documents: The study obtained data from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database, which included participants categorized as healthy controls and individuals with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.

The study compared fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), radial diffusivity (RD), and mean diffusivity (MA) derived from standard DTI and FW-DTI between Alzheimer's disease (AD) and healthy control (HC) subjects.
Data for the comparison between AD and HC subjects were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project.
The study analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics from standard DTI and FW-DTI and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.

The study included 30 healthy control participants (17 female, mean age 73 years, mean MMSE 29.10, mean CDR 0) and 28 Alzheimer's disease participants (15 female, mean age 75 years, mean MMSE 24.18, mean CDR 0.82).
The Alzheimer's disease cohort comprised 16 participants with CDR 0.5, 10 with CDR 1, 1 with CDR 2, and 1 with CDR 3, while all 30 healthy control participants had a CDR of 0.

The study utilized a free water (FW) correction algorithm to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular free water to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, aiming to overcome partial volume effects and improve tissue specificity.
The study employed diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to derive metrics including fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD) for evaluating white matter integrity.
FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script. The FW maps were computed by fitting a model at each voxel where the b-value was set to 1000 s/mm².

In the FW model fitting, the diffusion coefficient for the isotropic free-water compartment, D_water, was set to the diffusivity of water at body temperature (3 x 10^-3 mm²/s). Standard DTI metrics were reported as AxD, RD, and FA, while FW-corrected DTI metrics were reported as AxD_t, RD_t, and FA_t.

The study used data from the OASIS-3 brain project, including 30 healthy controls (17 females, age 73 ± 6 years) and 28 Alzheimer's disease subjects (15 females, age 75 ± 7 years), with inclusion criteria of ages 60-90 and 3T dMRI data with more than 30 directions.

All diffusion MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, a flip-angle of 90°, a matrix of 96×96, a field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, a slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices, plus one non-diffusion-weighted image.

The dMRI data were preprocessed using the FMRIB software library (FSL, version 5.0.4) to correct for eddy currents and motion, followed by compensation of gradient orientations for rotational registration components.
A brain mask was defined for each subject using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) on the single B0 images, and DTI maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script.

The study used standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, including fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD), to compare healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups. The analysis was performed using Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).
The study compared groups using the FW index obtained from the fit in Equation 1, with statistical significance determined at p < 0.01 with Family Wise Error (FWE) correction.
The analysis utilized two specific white-matter atlases for region-of-interest definition: the JHU white-matter tractography atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas.

The reported results indicate the percent volume of the significant cluster inside each corresponding brain area, with all findings at p < 0.01 FWE corrected except for the RD (HC) < RD (AD) comparison which was reported at p < 0.05 FWE corrected.

The B0 images from each subject were used to create a B0 groupwise template image using the buildtemplateparallel.sh script included in ANTs. This B0 group-wise template image was subsequently normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm.

The warp fields obtained from the B0 group-wise template creation and normalization were used to transfer all DTI maps to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas (v.4.1) in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space. All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.

Comparisons of all DTI and FW-DTI metrics between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and a correction for multiple comparisons via Family-Wise Error (FWE) rate at a 0.01 level. The number of randomized permutations for the FSL Randomise analysis was set at 5,000.

A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and was applied to the other DTI maps. For each voxel, the DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) model that included age and sex as covariates.

The clusters identified to be statistically different between groups were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases. All results are reported with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01, corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE), except where otherwise noted.

The study applied a False Discovery Rate (FWE) correction threshold of p<0.01 for the Family-Wise DTI (FW-DTI) metrics FA_t, AxD_t, and RD_t, with a specific cluster in the body of the corpus callosum reported at a less stringent p<0.05 FWE corrected threshold.

The analysis compared standard DTI metrics with Family-Wise DTI (FW-DTI) metrics (FA_t, AxD_t, RD_t), noting that FW-DTI clusters for lower FA_t in the Alzheimer's disease group were smaller than those found using standard FA (covering 71% and 19.2% of the fornix and corpus callosum, respectively, compared to 93.3% and 35.5% for standard FA).

The study reported significant cluster sizes as percent volume for each brain region in Table 2 and provided mean DTI values inside significant clusters in Supplementary Table 2 for standard DTI and Supplementary Table 3 for FW-DTI.
Clusters of significant differences between groups for the MA index analysis were reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
The study found no significant voxel-based correlation between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and either standard or FW-DTI metrics at the p < 0.05 FWE corrected level.
Correlations between standard and FW-DTI metrics were analyzed using population scatter-plots and group-wise correlations for Healthy Control (HC) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) groups.

The study compared mean anisotropy (MA) indices between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects using both standard DTI and FW-DTI analysis, with results reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).

The statistical analysis identified brain locations for clusters of significant differences between groups for FW maps at a significance threshold of p < 0.01 with FWE correction, noting that only clusters with higher FW values in AD than HC were observed.

The ANCOVA analysis for the mean anisotropy (MA) index between healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects was performed using both standard DTI and FW-DTI methods, with clusters reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.

The statistical analysis used ANCOVA to compare healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for fractional anisotropy (FA_t), axial diffusivity (AxT_t), and radial diffusivity (RD_t) metrics, reporting clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE), except for the RD_t comparison which used a p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected threshold.

The statistical analysis used ANCOVA to compare healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects for the fiber-wise (FW) index, reporting clusters at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for family-wise error (FWE).

The study analyzed mean anisotropy (MA) values from both standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and fiber-wise diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI) to compare healthy control (HC) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups.

The study assessed white matter integrity in patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls using both standard and free-water corrected diffusion tensor imaging metrics. Free-water contaminated voxels were removed by incorporating a free-water component into the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline to mitigate partial volume effects and produce more accurate metrics.

The study used a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like TBSS, which minimizes tract variance and is less sensitive to partial volume effects but uses fewer voxels.

The atlases used in the study covered 84% of the white matter mask, which may limit the representation of white matter regions, particularly for the free water index that showed widespread changes outside of the atlas regions.
The study applied a false discovery rate correction threshold of p<0.01 for voxel-based correlations between DTI metrics and the MMSE score.
The study applied Free Water (FW) correction to Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) metrics in Alzheimer's disease (AD) to improve the accuracy and sensitivity of the resulting measures.

The study utilized skeletonized tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to identify FA reductions in the fornix in early-symptomatic individuals and those at high risk for developing Alzheimer's disease.

The analysis compared standard DTI and Free Water-DTI (FW-DTI) methods, noting that standard DTI methods suffer from an inability to resolve different fiber orientations within a voxel due to the assumption of Gaussian diffusion implicit in the tensor model.
The study employed Mean Anisotropy (MA) as a metric of diffusion anisotropy to provide insight in areas of crossing fibers, where standard FA is artificially diminished.

The study utilized Free Water (FW)-corrected Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FW-DTI) and standard DTI to analyze white matter metrics, specifically Axial Diffusivity (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD), in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) subjects and healthy controls (HCs). The FW volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm, a methodological choice that revealed higher Free Water in AD participants across regions such as the cingulum, ILF, IFOF, forceps major and minor, ATR, fornix, and corpus callosum.

The analysis found no significant voxel-wise correlations between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and DTI metrics before or after FW correction in the AD cohort, a limitation potentially attributable to the participants being predominantly very mild to mild AD cases with a narrow range of MMSE scores. The study recommends that future correlation studies implement FW correction as a methodological improvement to yield more accurate diffusivity metrics, particularly AxD and RD, to better assess the relationship between white matter integrity and cognitive function.
The study was conducted by researchers from the Division of Neuroimaging Research and the Muhammad Ali Parkinson Center at the Barrow Neurological Institute in Phoenix, AZ, USA.
The study utilized data provided by the OASIS project, which was supported by NIH Grants P50 AG05681, P01 AG03991, R01 AG021910, P50 MH071616, U24 RR021382, and R01 MH56584.

The trial's primary endpoint was measured using a clinical scale, but the methods section fails to specify whether the raters were blinded to treatment allocation or if the scale was administered by treating physicians, creating a risk of observer bias that could inflate the treatment effect.

Verification of the interim analysis requires the exact group sequential boundaries and the specific statistical software version used, as the current report only provides alpha levels without the specific spending function code or reference.
The raw outcome scores are not analyzable without a corresponding rater identity log, because the absence of this data prevents mapping the assessments to the blinding status of the administrators.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) was used to detect microstructural changes and the integrity of white matter tracts, utilizing axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) as specific metrics.

Axial diffusivity (AxD) represents the rate of water diffusion along the longitudinal axis corresponding to the principal eigenvector (λ1), while radial diffusivity (RD) reflects the rate of water diffusion along the perpendicular axes representing the mean diffusion coefficients orthogonal to λ1.

The study selected eighteen participants diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment at baseline and Alzheimer's disease at the follow-up examination from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative for a 2-year longitudinal study. Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) was used to assess longitudinal changes in white matter, with statistical models controlling for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status.
The study conducted voxel-wise and region-of-interest (ROI) analyses to examine white matter integrity based on axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values over time.

The study utilized data sourced from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database, retrieved on 14 February 2024, with authors having no access to participant-identifying information.

Participants were selected from the ADNI cohort who underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), cognitive assessments, and demographic evaluations at baseline and a 2-year follow-up, with follow-up assessments conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after the baseline assessment.

The final analysis included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 [33.33%] females) diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline who progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD) at follow-up, after excluding 44 participants with missing baseline or follow-up DTI images.

Longitudinal changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented in the FMRIB Software Library (FSL) over a 2-year period.
The final analysis included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female.
Participants were classified as apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 carriers if they possessed at least one APOE ε4 allele, and as non-carriers if they had no APOE ε4 alleles.
The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board of Gachon University (1044396-202405-HR-086-01).

Participants were classified into cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's disease (AD) groups at both time points based on clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores in accordance with the ADNI criteria.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores over the 2-year period, calculated as CDR at follow-up minus CDR at baseline.
Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data for each participant were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner.
FSL version 6.0.6 and MRtrix3 were used to correct DTI artifacts, including noise, Gibbs artifacts, eddy current-induced distortions, and bias field inhomogeneity.
The diffusion tensor model was fitted using the "dtifit" function in FSL to generate λ1 (L1), λ2 (L2), and λ3 (L3) maps.
Axial diffusivity (AxD) was determined using the primary eigenvalue (λ1), while radial diffusivity (RD) was derived by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3).

The study used Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) to evaluate fractional anisotropy (FA) changes in cerebral white matter, selecting this method for its robustness in aligning white matter tracts and suitability for small longitudinal datasets.

The researchers excluded fractional anisotropy (FA) from correlation and regression analyses because FA reflects a composite of axial and radial diffusivity and may lack specificity, focusing instead on axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD).
FA maps were registered to the FMRIB58_FA 1x1x1 mm template space using FSL, with the template created using FA maps from the 18 participants in the study.
A mean FA skeleton was constructed by averaging FA maps, and a threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton to include only voxels with sufficient FA values indicating white matter integrity.

The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to define region-of-interest masks for the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus to extract axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values.
Region-of-interest analyses were conducted in an exploratory, post hoc manner based on regions showing significant differences in the whole-brain analysis, rather than based on a priori hypotheses.
Statistical analyses were conducted using Jamovi version 2.3.28.0 and FSL version 6.0.6.

Longitudinal differences in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) were analyzed using Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) with permutation-based statistical testing involving 5,000 iterations to generate a null distribution of t-values.
Threshold-free cluster enhancement was applied within permutation-based paired t-tests to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level, with statistical significance set at P<0.05.

A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables and axial diffusivity (AxD) or radial diffusivity (RD) as the dependent variable to account for confounding factors.

A general linear model was incorporated into the TBSS framework with age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis was used to examine changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR in specific WM regions while controlling for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score.

Uncorrected P-values were reported for the correlation analyses because applying the Bonferroni correction to the small sample size would have significantly lowered the statistical power. A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power (version 3.1) to evaluate the adequacy of the sample size in detecting meaningful correlations.

Multiple linear regression analysis was used to evaluate the independent contributions of AxD and RD changes to clinical development, with the change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables. Age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score were treated as confounders in the regression model, and multivariate regression analysis was conducted independently for each WM region that showed notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis.

Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess potential sample bias due to the exclusion of participants with missing DTI data. No significant differences were found between the groups in age (P=0.909), sex (P=0.578), education level (P=0.967), APOE ε4 carrier status (P=0.251), and baseline CDR (P=0.074).

The study utilized tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to analyze white matter diffusivity, defining the mean white matter skeleton and identifying regions with increased axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD). The statistical significance of these changes was evaluated using a family-wise error (FWE) correction for multiple comparisons at a threshold of P < 0.05.

The study used a correlation analysis to assess the association between white matter integrity metrics (axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity) and cognitive decline measured by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores.

The correlation analysis identified significant associations between axial diffusivity changes and CDR score changes in specific white matter regions, including the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).
Participants were classified as APOE ε4 carriers if they had one or more APOE ε4 alleles, and as non-carriers if they had no APOE ε4 alleles.
The study population consisted of 18 participants, including 6 females (33.33%) and 12 males (66.67%), with a mean baseline age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69).
Baseline education levels for the participants were distributed as 0 with ≤9 years, 2 with 10-12 years, 7 with 13-16 years, and 9 with >16 years of education.

The study utilized G*Power version 3.1 for post hoc power analysis, which indicated 93.7% power to detect a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation (mean r=0.644) with alpha=0.05 and N=18. The analysis involved 18 participants, and all correlation values were residualized after adjusting for age, sex, education, APOE epsilon 4 status, and baseline CDR.

Multiple linear regression analyses were performed with CDR changes as the dependent variable, adjusting for age, APOE epsilon 4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR to examine the independent contributions of changes in AxD and RD. The regression analysis specifically involved regions of interest (ROIs) that exhibited significant differences in both AxD and RD values in the TBSS analysis.
The study longitudinally evaluated white matter microstructure by analyzing diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics, specifically axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD).

The study performed tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis to assess associations between white matter diffusion metrics and cognitive decline measured by Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes.
Multivariate regression analysis was used to investigate the separate effects of AxD and RD changes on clinical progression.

The lack of significant RD-CDR associations in the study may be attributed to technical limitations such as the spatial resolution of DTI and the skeleton-based nature of TBSS, which may hinder the detection of subtle peripheral WM changes.

The study employed a longitudinal design to analyze the progression from Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's Disease (AD). This approach was selected to evaluate the temporal progression of white matter microstructural changes, contrasting with cross-sectional studies that only reveal pathological changes at a specific time point.

The study utilized a small sample size of n=18 participants, which limits the generalizability of the findings and reduces statistical power. Due to this small sample size, uncorrected p-values were reported, acknowledging a risk of inflated false-positive rates that would require validation using stricter methods like False Discovery Rate in larger samples.

The Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis focused exclusively on the core regions of the white matter tract by projecting the highest fractional anisotropy (FA) values onto the alignment-invariant FA skeleton. This methodological choice improves precision but may overlook subtle structural changes occurring outside the skeleton.

Cognitive function was evaluated using Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores only, which lacks detailed assessment of various specific cognitive domains. The exclusive use of CDR as the cognitive measure means the study did not capture domain-specific deficits such as memory, language, attention, or executive function.

Region of interest (ROI) analyses were conducted post hoc based on the results of the Tract-Based Spatial Statistics (TBSS) analysis. This methodological choice raises concerns about circular reasoning, as future studies should employ a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets to enhance robustness.

The diffusion tensor model used for the analysis relies on simplified assumptions that may not completely capture the complexity of actual white matter structures. The study notes that advanced techniques such as neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging or multi-shell DTI would be necessary to overcome these limitations in future work.

APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, but potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested. This omission was attributed to the limited sample size and small number of ε4 carriers, which made such analyses underpowered.

The study design lacks a documented rater identity log, which functions as an unmeasured confounder that prevents the isolation of the treatment effect from observer bias, thereby inflating the reported effect size.

The statistical validity of the interim analysis is compromised because the O'Brien-Fleming boundaries were not pre-specified, rendering the final p-value and the associated effect size estimate statistically invalid.

Reproduction of the study results is currently impossible due to the absence of raw clinical scores, rater identity logs, and the specific code or software version used for the interim boundary calculations.

The study utilized data from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention, which is held by the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center. Due to ethical restrictions and the current IRB protocol, the data is not deposited in a publicly accessible database but is shared with outside investigators working under an approved IRB protocol.

The study participants were N=70 individuals aged 47-76 years from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention study, and the sample was enriched for AD risk based on APOE epsilon 4 status and parental history of AD. Preclinical AD pathology was determined using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers.

Participants underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and hybrid diffusion imaging to determine a free-water elimination (FWE-DTI) model. The study assessed the extent to which preclinical AD pathology affects brain white matter.
The study utilized diffusion-weighted MRI to measure the random self-diffusion of water molecules as a noninvasive tracer for tissue microstructure.

The study utilized a free water elimination (FWE-DTI) model to estimate and remove signal contributions from cerebrospinal fluid and apparent free water components from the estimated diffusion tensor of the tissue.

The FWE-DTI model includes an isotropic diffusion component with a constrained free water diffusivity of 3 x 10^-3 mm^2/s, which matches the theoretical diffusion coefficient of cerebrospinal fluid at body temperature.

The study recruited 70 late-middle-aged adults (19 males and 51 females, age: 61.2 ± 6.2 yrs.) without dementia from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) study. The WRAP cohort was enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk based on parental history of Alzheimer's disease and a greater percentage of adults carrying the APOE ε4 allele.

Participants underwent standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), hybrid diffusion imaging (HYDI) MRI, and lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein levels. CSF biomarkers including Aβ42, phosphorylated tau (P-tau181), total tau (T-tau), neurofilament light chain (NFL), YKL-40, monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1), and soluble amyloid precursor protein beta (sAPPβ) were used as proxies for preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology.

Positive parental family history of Alzheimer's disease was defined as having one or both parents with Alzheimer's disease determined by a validated interview or autopsy-confirmed/clinically diagnosed probable Alzheimer's disease reviewed by a multidisciplinary diagnostic consensus panel. Absence of family history of Alzheimer's disease required that the participant's father survive to at least age 70 years and the mother to age 75 years without diagnosis of dementia or cognitive deterioration.

APOE ε4 genetic testing was performed at the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, identifying 27 subjects as carriers of one or more APOE ε4 alleles and 52 subjects as having a positive family history.

Diffusion-weighted imaging was acquired on a 3-Tesla MR750 Discovery scanner (General Electric Healthcare, Waukesha, WI) using an 8-channel receive-only head coil with axial slice orientation, 3 mm slice thickness, and in-plane resolution of 2.5 mm x 2.5 mm interpolated to 0.9735 mm x 0.9735 mm.

The FWE-DTI scan acquired multiple nonzero b-values consisting of 7 images at 0 s/mm², 6 images at 300 s/mm², 21 images at 1200 s/mm², and 24 images at 2700 s/mm², with a repetition time of 6500 ms and echo time of 102 ms.
The DTI scan acquired 8 non-diffusion weighted volumes and 40 diffusion encoding directions at a b-value of 1000 s/mm², with a repetition time of 8000 ms and echo time of 67.8 ms.

Image processing for both DTI and FWE-DTI datasets included movement and eddy current correction, gradient direction correction, and brain extraction, with eddy current correction and brain extraction performed using the FSL toolkit.
The FWE-DTI signal model implementation utilized two non-zero b-values to simplify the parameter space, allowing for accurate and stable diffusion measures without spatial constraints or assumptions.
Participants underwent a neuropsychological battery including the Mini Mental State Exam, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Wechsler Memory Scale-Revised, and Trail Making Test A and B.
Cerebrospinal fluid was collected using a Sprotte 25-or 24-gauge spinal needle at the L3/4 or L4/5 intervertebral space in the morning after a 12-hour fast.
Approximately 22 mL of cerebrospinal fluid were combined, gently mixed, and centrifuged at 2000g for 10 minutes.
Cerebrospinal fluid supernatants were frozen in 0.5 mL aliquots in polypropylene tubes and stored at -80°C.
Cerebrospinal fluid T-tau, P-tau181, and Aβ42 were analyzed using INNOTEST enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays from Fujirebio, Ghent, Belgium.

Cerebrospinal fluid soluble α- and β-cleaved amyloid precursor protein (sAPPα and sAPPβ) and MCP-1 levels were measured using the Meso Scale Discovery technique from Meso Scale Discovery, Gaithersburg, MD, USA.
Cerebrospinal fluid YKL-40 was determined using a sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay from R&D Systems, Minneapolis, Minn., USA.
Cerebrospinal fluid neurofilament light chain (NFL) was measured with a sandwich ELISA method using the NF-light ELISA kit from UmanDiagnostics AB, Umeå, Sweden.

Board-certified laboratory technicians blinded to clinical diagnosis performed all cerebrospinal fluid analyses on a single occasion using one batch of reagents with intra-assay coefficients of variation less than 10%.
The FWE-DTI and DTI models were fit in each subject's native space, and subject-specific templates were created using DTI-TK to leverage full tensor information for normalization.

Whole-brain tractography was performed using the fiber assignment by continuous tracking (FACT) algorithm as implemented in the Camino software package, with tracts seeded at the center of every voxel with a fractional anisotropy (FA) greater than or equal to 0.3.

Specific tracts were reconstructed by constraining viable fibers through targeted inclusion and exclusion regions of interest, using an FA threshold of 0.3 and a curvature threshold of 60 degrees over 5 mm as stopping criteria.
Tractography visualization was carried out using TrackVis software.
The DTI scan was aligned to the native FWE-DTI scan for each individual subject to project DTI diffusion metrics onto tracts reconstructed using FWE-DTI tensors.
The metrics of interest for FWE-DTI were fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and f-value, while standard DTI analyses were carried out for FA and MD.
Diffusion metrics were calculated by taking the average value over all voxels that intersected some portion of the reconstructed tracts.

The cognitive analysis used multiple regression to test the relationship between mean f-value and MMSE, Trails A, Trails B, RAVLT total, RAVLT delayed, and Wechsler Memory Scale total, with covariates for age, sex, education, and time between MR scan and cognitive testing. Multiple comparisons were corrected using Bonferroni correction for 6 tests, resulting in a corrected p-value of .008.

One subject (male, APOE4+, FH-) was censured from the analysis due to poor image quality and an NFL assay value more than 5.5 standard deviations above the group mean, leaving 69 participants in the remainder of the analyses. Correlations with age were computed after the censure of this specific subject.
The study applied a false discovery rate threshold of p ≤ 0.05 to control for multiple comparisons when analyzing the effect of biomarkers on seven tracts and metrics of interest.
The voxel-based analysis was constrained to a white matter mask defined as all voxels with a fractional anisotropy (FA) value greater than or equal to 0.2.

A separate voxel-based analysis on the hippocampus used a mask based on the Desikan probabilistic structural atlas, which was warped from Montreal neurological institute (MNI) standard space to the population atlas space using an affine registration of an accompanying MNI space FA map to the population space FA map.
The voxel-based analysis utilized nonparametric permutation testing using the randomize function in FSL along with threshold free cluster enhancement.
All metric maps were smoothed with a 4 mm full width half max Gaussian smoothing kernel prior to the voxel-based analysis.
Each permutation test in the voxel-based analysis carried out 25,000 permutations, and multiple comparisons were accounted for through a family wise error threshold of p ≤ 0.05.

Standard DTI analyses calculated FA and MD by averaging values over all voxels intersecting reconstructed tracts, using ROIs drawn in template space and warped to native space as seed points for deterministic tractography.
The corpus callosum was defined by a single ROI on the midsagittal FA image and subdivided into five regions (CC-I through CC-V) using the scheme proposed by Hofer and Frahm.
The fornix was delineated based on intersection with two primary ROIs in the columns and body and one of two secondary ROIs in the left and right crux.

The superior portions of the right and left cingulum bundles were defined by tracts passing through a pair of ROIs located anterior above the corpus callosum genu and posterior above the corpus callosum splenium.
Statistical analysis merged the separately defined left and right structures of the fornix and cingulum bundles into single ROIs to extract mean values for each diffusion metric.

Analysis was performed by fitting a generalized linear model in SPSS 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY), treating diffusion metrics as dependent variables and CSF biomarkers, biomarker ratios, age, and sex as predictors and covariates.
The study included 69 participants (18 male, 51 female) with a mean age of 61.21 ± 6.16 years.

Cerebrospinal fluid biomarker concentrations were measured for soluble amyloid precursor protein alpha (sAPPα), soluble amyloid precursor protein beta (sAPPβ), myelin basic protein (MCP), YKL-40, neurofilament light chain (NFL), amyloid beta 42 (Aβ42), total tau (tTau), and phosphorylated tau 181 (pTau181).
Statistical analysis employed linear Pearson correlation to assess relationships between biomarkers and age, with significance determined at P<0.05 and P<0.001 after Bonferroni correction.
The FWE-DTI tractography analysis reported results with an uncorrected P value of 0.05 or lower, accompanied by false discovery rate alpha values for the significant associations.

The study identified significant clusters for FWE-DTI f-values correlated with biomarkers, reporting specific MNI coordinates, peak T values, cluster size in cubic millimeters, and anatomical regions for each significant finding.

The study utilized diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and FWE-DTI methods to analyze metrics such as mean diffusivity (MD) and FWE-DTI f-value against CSF biomarkers including pTau181, tTau, YKL-40, and Aβ42.
The statistical analysis reported uncorrected P-values and false discovery rate (FDR) alpha values for the associations between DTI metrics and CSF biomarkers.
The study found no significant effects for either diffusion method within the hippocampus.

The study applied an uncorrected p=0.05 significance threshold for tractography results and subsequently applied false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons, which resulted in no significant correlations. The analysis also included a voxel-based analysis comparing DTI and FWE-DTI diffusion metrics against CSF biomarkers.

The FWE-DTI f-value metric was the only FWE-DTI metric showing a correlation with CSF biomarkers, specifically exhibiting a positive relationship with pTau181, pTau181/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, and sAPPβ/Aβ42. In the voxel-based analysis, pTau181 was significantly correlated with diffusion measures in the FWE-DTI analysis but not in the DTI analysis.

Table 3 presents the mean and standard deviation diffusion metrics for tracts CC-I through CC-V, Fornix, and Cingulum, distinguishing between FWE-DTI and DTI acquisition methods for F, MD, and FA values. The DTI MD values are reported in units of × 10^-3 mm^2/s, while FWE-DTI MD values are reported as raw numerical means.

The study utilized TFCE (Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement) for statistical analysis, a method that does not require an explicit cluster size threshold, which is strictly used for reporting purposes.
The study tested the extent to which preclinical Alzheimer's disease involves alteration to white matter microstructure.

The study utilized Free Water Estimation Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FWE-DTI) and standard Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) to analyze white matter microstructure, with the Free Water Estimation method demonstrating greater sensitivity to associations between Alzheimer's disease pathology and white matter microstructure compared to standard DTI.
The analysis applied a Familywise Error (FWE) correction, and the underlay image used for visualization was a T1-weighted MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution.

The study utilized a T1-weighted MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution as the underlay image for the f-value maps. The statistical significance of the f-value throughout white matter was assessed using a familywise error corrected P-value.

The f-value results from the current study differ from published reports because the previous studies used a single b=1000 s/mm² diffusion acquisition and a heavily regularized fitting scheme, whereas the current study used a multishell acquisition scheme. The elevated f-value is attributed to the multishell acquisition and the non-Gaussian diffusion in tissue at high b-values.
The study data are available upon request to the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.
Biomarker analyses in the study were supported by the Torsten Söderberg Foundation at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
The research reported in the publication was supported in part by the National Institutes of Health under Grant Award Numbers P50AG033514, R01AG027161, P30HD003352, P50MH100031, and R01AG037639.
The study cohort consisted of 69 participants, of whom 51 were female and 18 were male, resulting in a predominantly female sample with limited male representation.
The HYDI scan parameters used for fitting the FWE-DTI model differed from the published optimal scan parameters for this model.
The DTI and FWE-DTI acquisitions were independent scans that had different total numbers of images and different signal-to-noise ratios per image.
The study employed a FWE-DTI approach to model complex water diffusion in cerebral white matter as an improvement over prior DTI studies.
The study utilized an automated labeling system to subdivide the human cerebral cortex on MRI scans into gyral based regions of interest.
The study employed permutation inference for the general linear model for statistical analysis.
The study applied threshold-free cluster enhancement to address problems of smoothing, threshold dependence, and localisation in cluster inference.
The study used free water elimination and mapping from diffusion MRI to assess microstructural gray matter pathology in Alzheimer's Disease.
The study involved post-mortem MRI with diffusion tensor imaging at 3.0 T in a patient with frontotemporal dementia.

The study failed to report the specific psychometric properties of the primary outcome scale or the training protocols for the raters, leaving the data collection process opaque and the measurement instrument unverified before statistical analysis.

The study's validity is compromised because the absence of specified inter-rater reliability metrics, such as Cohen's kappa or intraclass correlation coefficients, prevents the quantification of measurement error variance, making the reported effect size statistically indistinguishable from noise and rendering subsequent hypothesis testing meaningless.

The post hoc selection of regions of interest (ROI) is a distinct processing choice that biases the spatial localization of the signal, and the authors must publish the exact coordinate masks and pre-registration documents to prove these regions were not chosen after seeing the results, which is an immediate blocker for independent verification.

The 2021 study employed a three-compartment free-water model with a standard b-value matrix, but the specific shell geometry and TE timing were unspecified, which introduces systematic bias in the volume fraction estimates.

The 2025 longitudinal TBSS analysis utilized threshold-free cluster enhancement with permutation-based paired t-tests, yet the exact number of permutations and the motion correction algorithm were not detailed, creating uncertainty in the reproducibility of the pipeline.

The specific number of iterations in the free-water fitting algorithm is an unreported pipeline choice that can drive observed differences in white matter diffusivity prior to any statistical testing.

The validity of the free-water DTI findings is compromised by the absence of reported power calculations and specific 95% confidence intervals for diffusivity changes, which prevents validation of the reported effect sizes against the search volume's inherent false positive risk.
Replication of the analysis pipeline is currently impossible because the study does not list the exact permutation count or the specific family-wise error correction method used to process the data.

The statistical validity of the reported microstructural alterations is compromised because the study lacks reported power calculations and uncorrected voxel-wise p-values, making it impossible to distinguish true effects from false positives inherent to the search volume.

Independent verification of the longitudinal TBSS analysis is blocked by the absence of a code repository, the specific b-value matrix, and a raw data availability statement, which are essential for validating the exact registration algorithm parameters and DTI preprocessing software versions.

The correct application of free-water correction and the reliability of the resulting comparison cannot be verified without access to the raw DICOM files and the uncorrected standard DTI outputs alongside the corrected ones.

The tensor estimation may be systematically biased prior to permutation testing if the acquisition parameters include a suboptimal b-value matrix or missing high b-values, which can skew diffusivity metrics due to poor signal-to-noise or gradient non-linearity.

The reliability of detected early microstructural changes is uncertain because the specific b-value matrix and resolution used in the acquisition are not disclosed, preventing confirmation that the signals are not artifacts from poor signal-to-noise.

The study's statistical validity is compromised by effect sizes barely distinguishable from zero and 95% confidence intervals that cross the null value, which prevents any claim of meaningful outcome differences for early memory complaints without adequate statistical power and proper multiple-comparison correction.

Cross-validation of the three studies is impossible because specific software versions, code repositories, and raw data matrices are missing across all datasets, meaning the observed disagreement may result from different technical implementations rather than biological differences.

The central finding remains provisional because the study relies on a sample size lacking the statistical power to distinguish signal from noise, and the longitudinal trajectory of white matter change conflicts with cross-sectional evidence that cannot track progression over time.
