documents: The study data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls and mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease participants.

The study compared FA, AxD, RD, and MA from standard DTI and FW-DTI between AD and HC subjects using data from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project. The study also analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score.
The study cohort consists of 30 healthy controls (17 female, mean age 73) and 28 Alzheimer's disease patients (15 female, mean age 75).
The healthy control group had a mean MMSE score of 29.10 and a mean CDR score of 0, while the Alzheimer's disease group had a mean MMSE score of 24.18 and a mean CDR score of 0.82.
The Alzheimer's disease group CDR distribution includes 16 subjects at CDR 0.5, 10 at CDR 1, 1 at CDR 2, and 1 at CDR 3, whereas all 30 healthy controls are at CDR 0.
The analysis utilizes diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to derive fractional anisotropy (FA), axial diffusivity (AxD), and radial diffusivity (RD) metrics.
A free water correction algorithm is applied to DTI-derived metrics to remove the contribution of extracellular free water and improve tissue specificity.
The FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script that is available upon request. The FW maps were computed by fitting a specific model at each voxel.

The FW model fitting uses a b-value of 1000 s/mm² and sets the diffusion coefficient D_water to 3 x 10⁻³ mm²/s. The model parameters include the diffusion tensor D, fractional volume f, and applied diffusion gradient g.

The mode of anisotropy (MA) is calculated using the DTI eigenvalues λ1, λ2, and λ3 via the provided mathematical formula. MA is mathematically orthogonal to FA and relates to the skewness of the DTI eigenvalues.
The study data were sourced from the OASIS-3 brain project (http://oasis-brains.org/), a freely available neuroimaging dataset for normal aging and Alzheimer's disease.

The dMRI data were acquired on a 3 T Siemens scanner using 64 diffusion-encoding directions with a b-value of 1000 s/mm², TR/TE of 11,000/87.0 ms, flip-angle of 90°, matrix of 96×96, field of view of 24.0 × 24.0 cm, slice thickness of 2.5 mm, and 64 axial slices.

The dMRI data were preprocessed using the FMRIB software library tool (FSL, version 5.0.4) for eddy current and motion correction, and a brain mask was defined using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) for single B0 images.
DTI standard and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script that is available upon request, with FW maps computed by fitting a specific model at each voxel.

FW-DTI analysis results are reported at a significance threshold of p < 0.01 FWE corrected, with the exception of a specific cluster in the body of the corpus callosum showing higher RD_t in the AD group at p < 0.05 FWE corrected.

The specific quantitative data for mean DTI values inside significant clusters are located in Supplementary Table 2, and the mean FW-DTI values inside significant clusters are located in Supplementary Table 3.
The significant cluster sizes expressed as percent volume for each brain region are reported in Table 2.
The simultaneous alteration of multiple DTI metrics between HC and AD groups is detailed in Supplementary Table 1.
The ANCOVA analysis between Healthy Control and Alzheimer's Disease subjects for standard DTI metrics uses a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).
The specific cluster sizes, expressed as percent volume for each brain region, are reported in Table 2, and regions with simultaneously altered DTI metrics are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

The statistical comparisons between Healthy Control and Alzheimer's Disease groups for age and sex showed no significant differences (t=0.233; p=0.817), while MMSE (t=-5.21; p<0.0001) and CDR (t=-8.22; p<0.0001) showed significant differences.
B0 images from each subject were used to create a B0 groupwise template image using the buildtemplateparallel.sh script included in ANTs.
The B0 group-wise template image was normalized to the IIT_mean_b0 image using the ANTs symmetric image normalization (SyN) algorithm.

Warp fields from the B0 group-wise template creation and normalization were used to transfer all DTI maps to the Illinois Institute of Technology (IIT) Human Brain Atlas version 4.1, which is in International Consortium for Brain Mapping (ICBM)-152 space.
All DTI maps in standard space were smoothed using FSL with an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a sigma of 3 mm.
Comparisons of DTI metrics and maps between groups were performed using the FSL Randomise tool with threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) and Family-Wise Error (FWE) correction at a 0.01 level.
A white matter mask was defined using a threshold of 0.2 on the average values of fractional anisotropy (FA) from standard DTI and applied to the other DTI maps.
For each voxel, DTI-derived metrics were fitted by an Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) model that included age and sex as covariates.
The number of randomized permutations for the FSL Randomise tool was set at 5,000.
Statistically different clusters were labeled according to the Johns Hopkins University (JHU) DTI-based white-matter atlases.

The voxel-based relationship between MMSE scores and DTI metrics for the Alzheimer's disease group was assessed using FSL Randomise with a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family-Wise Error (FWE).

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas defines specific regions including CC (corpus callosum), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiate), SS (sagittal stratum), and SFOF (superior fronto-occipital fasciculus).

FW-DTI metric clusters in the ANCOVA analysis between HC and AD subjects are reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE, except for RD_t (HC) < RD_t (AD), which is reported at p-value < 0.05 FWE-corrected.
FW index clusters in the ANCOVA analysis between HC and AD subjects are reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.
The complete list of group-wise significant clusters for the FW index between HC and AD is reported in Table 3.
The complete list of group-wise significant clusters for the MA index between HC and AD is reported in Table 4.
Significant differences between groups were identified using the FW index obtained from the fit in Eq. 1 at a threshold of p<0.01 FWE corrected.
The analysis found only clusters with higher FW values in the AD group compared with the HC group.
The reported percent volume values in Table 2 correspond to the percent volume of the cluster inside the corresponding brain area.
All results in Table 2 are shown for p<0.01 (FWE corrected), except for the column indicating RD (HC) < RD (AD), which is reported at p<0.05 (FWE corrected).

The JHU white-matter tractography atlas abbreviations are: ATR anterior thalamic radiation, CST cortical spinal tract, CGC cingulum (cingulate gyrus part), CGH cingulum (hippocampal part), IFOF inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, ILF inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and UF uncinate fasciculus.

The ICBM-DTI-81 white-matter atlas abbreviations are: CC corpus callosum, LIC limb of internal capsule, IC internal capsule, CR corona radiate, SS sagittal stratum, and SFOF superior fronto-occipital fasciculus.
The study used a conventional diffusion modeling pipeline incorporating a free-water component to remove free water-contaminated voxels and produce FW-corrected DTI metrics.
The specific parameters derived from the free-water correction were FW-corrected FA (FA_t), FW-corrected AxD (AxD_t), FW-corrected RD (RD_t), and the FW index.
The study assessed white matter integrity in patients with Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls using both standard and free-water-corrected DTI metrics.
The study used the JHU WM tract. atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas to define brain regions for the MA index analysis.
Clusters of significant differences in the MA index were reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for Family Wise Error (FWE).
The percentage columns in Table 4 indicate the percent volume of the significant cluster inside the corresponding brain area for the standard and FW-MA analyses.
No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and either standard or FW-DTI metrics at the p<0.05 FWE corrected level.
The correlation between Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Axial Diffusivity (AxD) in the AD group increased from 0.160 (standard) to 0.856 (FW-corrected).
The correlation between Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) in the AD group changed from -0.464 (standard) to -0.803 (FW-corrected).

Table 4 reports the complete list of group-wise significant clusters for the FW (HC) and FW (AD) groups, including the percentage volume and mean values for white matter tracts defined by the JHU WM tract atlas and the ICBM-DTI-81 WM atlas.

Table 3 lists brain locations with significant differences between groups for FW maps analysis at a significance threshold of p < 0.01 corrected for FWE, where the percentage columns indicate the percent volume of the cluster inside the corresponding brain area.

The JHU white matter tractography atlas abbreviations are defined as ATR (anterior thalamic radiation), CST (cortical spinal tract), CGC (cingulum cingulate gyrus part), CGH (cingulum hippocampal part), IFOF (inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus), ILF (inferior longitudinal fasciculus), SLF (superior longitudinal fasciculus), and UF (uncinate fasciculus).

The ICBM-DTI-81 white matter atlas abbreviations are defined as CC (corpus callosum), CP (cerebral peduncle), LIC (limb of internal capsule), IC (internal capsule), CR (corona radiata), SS (sagittal stratum), and EC (external capsule).

Figure 4 displays a coronal view of the ANCOVA analysis between HC and AD subjects for the MA index derived from standard DTI and FW-DTI, with clusters reported at a significance threshold of p-value < 0.01 corrected for FWE.

The free water (FW) volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm, with specific percentages reported for the cingulum hippocampal part (85.16%), cingulate gyrus part (56.34%), ILF (52%), IFOF (40%), forceps major and minor (approximately 40% each), ATR (31.39%), fornix (95.6%), and CC genu, body, and splenium (approximately 56% of total CC).

Approximately 42% of the free water (FW) clusters were located in white matter outside the regions specified by the atlases, with FW increases specifically found in several regions bordering various sulcal fundi.

No significant voxel-wise correlations were observed between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics before or after free water (FW) correction in the Alzheimer's disease cohort, a gap attributed to the predominantly very mild to mild AD group characteristics and the relatively narrow range of MMSE scores.
The study used a voxel-based approach for white matter analysis rather than a skeletonized approach like TBSS, and the atlases used covered 84% of the white matter mask.
The study applied a voxel-based correlation threshold of p<0.01 with FWE correction when analyzing the relationship between DTI metrics and the MMSE score.
The data for the study was provided by the OASIS project, which is supported by NIH Grants P50 AG05681, P01 AG03991, R01 AG021910, P50 MH071616, U24 RR021382, and R01 MH56584.
Supplementary material for the article is available online at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-86505-7.

The exact group sequential boundaries and the specific statistical software version used for the interim analysis are required to verify the final results, as the provided alpha levels are insufficient without the specific spending function code or reference.

Replication is blocked by the lack of specification regarding whether the primary endpoint was measured using a standardized clinical scale and whether it was administered by blinded raters or treating physicians, as this observer bias could inflate the treatment effect independently of the statistical spending function.

The methods section omits the specific psychometric properties of the clinical scale and the training protocols for the raters, creating a gap that prevents ruling out observer expectation bias in the outcome data acquisition.
The raw scores are unusable for replication without the corresponding rater identity log, because the absence of this log prevents mapping the data back to the blinding status of the assessments.
The study utilized 18 participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline and AD at follow-up, selected from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative, for a 2-year longitudinal analysis.
The statistical models controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status during the voxel-wise and region-of-interest analyses.
All relevant data are available within the manuscript and its Supporting Information files.

The study used data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database (adni.loni.usc.edu) retrieved on 14 February 2024. The analysis included 18 participants (age 72.00 ± 8.69; 6 [33.33%] females) who were diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) at baseline and progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD) at the follow-up examination.

Longitudinal changes in axonal damage (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) were evaluated using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) implemented with the FMRIB Software Library (FSL) over a 2-year period. Follow-up assessments were conducted at 24.78 ± 1.75 months after the baseline assessment.

Participants with missing baseline or follow-up diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) images were excluded from the analysis. The final cohort consisted of 18 participants after excluding 44 participants due to missing imaging data.
The final analysis included 18 participants with a mean age of 72.00 ± 8.69 years, of whom 6 (33.33%) were female.
Participants with at least one apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele were classified as carriers, while those with no APOE ε4 alleles were classified as non-carriers.
The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Institutional Review Board of Gachon University (1044396-202405-HR-086-01).
Dementia severity was assessed using the clinical dementia rating (CDR), which combines data from patient and caregiver interviews across six cognitive domains.

Participants were classified into cognitively normal, MCI, and AD groups at both time points based on CDR scores in accordance with the ADNI criteria available at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/methods/documents/.
Cognitive decline was defined as the change in CDR scores over the 2-year period, calculated as CDR at follow-up minus CDR at baseline.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) data were acquired using a 3T MRI scanner, with detailed imaging protocols described in publicly available documents at https://adni.loni.usc.edu/methods/documents/mri-protocols.

FSL version 6.0.6 (http://www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl) and MRtrix3 (https://www.mrtrix.org) were used to correct DTI artifacts including noise, Gibbs artifacts, eddy current-induced distortions, and bias field inhomogeneity.
The diffusion tensor model was fitted using the "dtifit" function in FSL to generate λ1, λ2, and λ3 maps.
Axial diffusivity (AxD) was determined using the primary eigenvalue (λ1), while radial diffusivity (RD) was derived by averaging the secondary eigenvalues (λ2 and λ3).
The study used FSL version 6.0.6 and Jamovi version 2.3.28.0 for statistical analysis and processing.
TBSS analysis registered FA maps to the FMRIB58_FA 1x1x1 mm template created from the 18 participants' FA maps.
A mean FA skeleton was constructed and refined using a threshold of 0.2 to include only voxels with sufficient fractional anisotropy.
Permutation testing used 5,000 iterations to generate a null distribution of t-values for the TBSS analysis.
Statistical significance was set at P<0.05 using threshold-free cluster enhancement-corrected P-values.
A general linear model included age, sex, education, and APOE epsilon 4 status as independent variables with AxD and RD as dependent variables.
Region-of-interest masks for the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus were derived from the Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas.
The ROI analyses were conducted post hoc based on significant regions from the TBSS whole-brain analysis rather than a priori hypotheses.

The general linear model incorporated into the TBSS framework used age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status as independent variables and AxD/RD as the dependent variable. Spearman's correlation analysis controlled for age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score while examining changes in ROI-based AxD, RD, and CDR.

A post hoc power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1 to evaluate sample size adequacy. Uncorrected P-values were reported for correlation analyses because applying the Bonferroni correction would have significantly lowered statistical power due to the small sample size.

Multiple linear regression analysis evaluated the independent contributions of AxD and RD changes to clinical development, with change in CDR scores as the dependent variable and AxD and RD as independent variables. Age, sex, education, APOE ε4 status, and baseline CDR score were treated as confounders in the regression model, which was conducted independently for each WM region showing notable variations in AxD or RD in the TBSS analysis.

The CDR score increased from a mean of 2.42 ± 1.17 at baseline to 4.64 ± 1.44 at follow-up over 2 years (P < 0.001). Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared between the included group (n=18) and the excluded group (n=44) to assess sample bias due to missing DTI data, with no significant differences found in age, sex, education level, APOE ε4 carrier status, or baseline CDR.

Table 2 reports the specific voxel sizes for significant changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) across 30 white matter regions, including the splenium of corpus callosum (1625 voxels for AxD, 1387 for RD) and the superior longitudinal fasciculus (1025 voxels for AxD, 1171 for RD).

The tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis identified that decreased diffusivity metrics (AxD and RD) exhibited no statistically significant differences at P<0.05 after correcting for multiple comparisons using family-wise error (FWE).

The study reports significant correlations between axial diffusivity (AxD) changes and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score changes in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule (r=0.704, P=0.007), left posterior corona radiata (r=0.676, P=0.011), left fornix cres stria terminalis (r=0.627, P=0.022), and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (r=0.568, P=0.043).

Table 3 provides the complete correlation coefficients (r) and p-values for axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) across all listed white matter regions, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, and various fasciculi.
The data table defines AxD as axial diffusivity, RD as radial diffusivity, CDR as clinical dementia rating, and uses R and L to denote right and left hemispheres, respectively.

The study population consisted of 18 participants (6 female, 12 male) with a mean age of 72.00 years (SD 8.69) at baseline, where 6 participants (33.33%) were APOE ε4 carriers and 12 (66.67%) were non-carriers.
Baseline education levels included 2 participants (11.11%) with 10-12 years, 7 participants (38.89%) with 13-16 years, and 9 participants (50.00%) with more than 16 years of education.
The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score increased from a baseline mean of 2.42 (SD 1.17) to a follow-up mean of 4.64 (SD 1.44), representing a statistically significant change (P < 0.001).
Participants with one or more APOE ε4 alleles were classified as carriers, while those with zero APOE ε4 alleles were classified as non-carriers.

The post hoc power analysis for the study used G*Power version 3.1 with an alpha of 0.05 and N=18, indicating 93.7% power to detect a correlation of r=0.704 and 86.3% power for the average observed correlation of r=0.644.
The multiple linear regression analysis used CDR changes as the dependent variable and adjusted for age, APOE ε4 status, education, sex, and baseline CDR.
The regression analysis included regions of interest exhibiting significant differences in both AxD and RD values in the TBSS analysis.
The results of the regression analysis for all regions of interest are summarized in S2 Table.
The study utilized diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) to measure anisotropic diffusion metrics, specifically axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), as indicators of white matter integrity.

Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis identified significant changes in AxD and RD in the corpus callosum (CC), cingulum bundle (CR), cingulate gyrus (CG), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), and internal capsule (IC).
The regression analysis results for all regions of interest (ROIs) are summarized in S2 Table.
The study utilized diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) to analyze axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) changes.
The study correlated diffusion metric changes with Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores to assess cognitive decline.

The specific white matter regions examined for correlations with CDR changes were the left retrolenticular region of the internal capsule (IC), left posterior corona radiata (PCR), left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF).
The study employed multivariate regression analysis to investigate the separate effects of AxD and RD changes on clinical progression.

The study found that AxD changes in the left retrolenticular region of the IC, left PCR, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right SLF exhibited significant correlations with changes in CDR scores.
The study found no significant correlations between radial diffusivity (RD) changes and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) changes across any of the examined white matter regions.
The study identified technical limitations in detecting subtle peripheral white matter changes due to the spatial resolution of DTI and the skeleton-based nature of TBSS.

Supporting data for the study includes S1 table containing AxD and RD changes in white matter ROIs for individual participants and S2 table containing ROI-wise multivariate regression analysis of AxD and RD changes on CDR score changes, both provided in XLSX format.
The study utilizes data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), with a complete listing of ADNI investigators available in S3 File (PDF).
The study utilized a small sample size (n=18) and reported uncorrected p-values, which limits generalizability and increases the risk of inflated false-positive rates.

Cognitive function was evaluated exclusively using Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, lacking detailed assessment of specific cognitive domains such as memory, language, attention, and executive function.

Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis focused only on core white matter regions projected onto the FA skeleton, potentially overlooking subtle structural changes occurring outside the skeleton.

Region of interest (ROI) analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, raising concerns about circular reasoning and the need for a priori ROI definitions or independent validation datasets.

The diffusion tensor model relies on simplified assumptions that may not fully capture the complexity of actual white matter structures, necessitating the use of advanced techniques like neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging or multi-shell DTI for future replication.

Although APOE ε4 status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, potential interaction effects between ε4 status and white matter changes were not tested due to limited sample size and a small number of ε4 carriers.

Reproducibility of AxD metrics requires standardization across imaging protocols and scanners, as well as the establishment of normative datasets to define AxD thresholds indicative of pathological changes.
Reference 34 (Bach et al., 2014) provides methodological considerations for tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) analysis, which is a specific analytical technique used in the study.
Reference 22 (Bergamino et al., 2021) describes the use of free-water diffusion tensor imaging to improve the accuracy and sensitivity of white matter analysis in Alzheimer's disease.
Reference 32 (Saito et al., 2023) addresses the reproducibility of an automated calculation technique for diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space.
Reference 39 (Qi et al., 2024) utilizes a cross-sectional tract-based spatial statistics and fixel-based analysis approach to assess cerebral white matter injury.
Reference 45 (Dou et al., 2020) employs an automated fiber quantification analysis method to characterize white matter connectivity using two independent datasets.
Reference 48 (Li et al., 2024) applies the tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) method for diffusion kurtosis imaging of brain white matter alterations.
Reference 66 (Liu et al., 2020) utilizes a DTI study using TBSS analysis to identify micro-structural white matter abnormalities.
Reference 71 (Reijmer et al., 2012) employs spherical deconvolution based tractography to improve sensitivity to cerebral white matter abnormalities in Alzheimer's disease.
Reference 72 (Kincses et al., 2013) identifies patterns of diffusion parameter changes in Alzheimer's disease using Linked Independent Component Analysis.

The specific code or software version used for the O'Brien-Fleming interim boundary calculations is missing, which blocks verification of whether the multiplicity adjustment was pre-specified and statistically valid.

The missing rater identity log constitutes an unmeasured confounder that prevents the separation of the treatment effect from rater bias, rendering the reported effect size unreproducible without this specific artifact.

Data from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's prevention is available from the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, which may be contacted at adrc@medicine.wisc.edu. Due to ethical restrictions, the data is not deposited to a database, and the LEAD data cannot be deposited in a publicly accessible database under the current IRB protocol.

The work is made available under the Creative Commons CCO public domain dedication, allowing it to be freely reproduced, distributed, transmitted, modified, built upon, or otherwise used by anyone for any lawful purpose.

The study included 70 participants aged 47-76 years from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention study who underwent diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and hybrid diffusion imaging to determine a free-water elimination (FWE-DTI) model.

Preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology was determined using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers in a sample enriched for Alzheimer's disease risk via APOE ε4 status and parental history of Alzheimer's disease.
Data and tissue requests are reviewed by Dr. Barbara Bendlin, who confirms IRB approval or exemption (protocol #2015-1450) before release.

Investigators outside the University of Washington system must follow HIPAA procedures, and only coded data or samples without access to the code are transferred via secure methods such as sFTP or Box.
Research reported in the publication was supported by National Institutes of Health Grant Award Numbers P50AG033514, R01AG027161, P30HD003352, P50MH100031, and R01AG037639.
Biomarker analyses in the project were supported by the Torsten Söderberg Foundation at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
The study recruited 70 late-middle-aged adults (19 males, 51 females, mean age 61.2 ± 6.2 years) without dementia from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) study.

Participants underwent standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), hybrid diffusion imaging (HYDI) MRI, and lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers including Aβ42, P-tau181, T-tau, neurofilament light chain (NFL), YKL-40, monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1), and soluble amyloid precursor protein beta (sAPPβ).
APOE ε4 genetic testing was performed at the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, identifying 27 subjects as carriers of one or more APOE ε4 alleles.

Positive parental family history of Alzheimer's disease was defined by having one or both parents with Alzheimer's disease as determined by a validated interview or autopsy-confirmed/clinically diagnosed probable Alzheimer's disease, reviewed by a multidisciplinary diagnostic consensus panel.
CSF was collected using a Sprotte 25-or 24-gauge spinal needle at the L3/4 or L4/5 intervertebral space into polypropylene syringes in the morning after a 12h fast.
Approximately 22mL of CSF were centrifuged at 2000g for 10 minutes, and the supernatants were frozen in 0.5 mL aliquots in polypropylene tubes and stored at -80°C.
CSF T-tau, P-tau181, and Aβ42 were analyzed using INNOTEST enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays from Fujiurebio, Ghent Belgium.
CSF soluble α- and β-cleaved amyloid precursor protein (sAPPα and sAPPβ) and MCP-1 levels were measured using the Meso Scale Discovery technique from Meso Scale Discovery, Gaithersburg, MD, USA.
CSF YKL-40 was determined using a sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) from R&D Systems, Minneapolis, Minn., USA.
CSF neurofilament light chain (NFL) was measured with a sandwich ELISA method using the NF-light ELISA kit from UmanDiagnostics AB, Umeå, Sweden.

All CSF biomarker analyses were performed on one occasion by blinded technicians using one batch of reagents according to protocols approved by the Swedish Board of Accreditation and Conformity Assessment (SWEDAC), with intra-assay coefficients of variation less than 10%.
Participants underwent a neuropsychological battery including the Mini Mental State Exam, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Wechsler Memory Scale-Revised, and Trail Making Test A and B.

Standard DTI analyses calculated FA and MD by averaging values over all voxels intersecting reconstructed tracts, using ROIs drawn in template space and warped to native space for deterministic tractography. The corpus callosum was defined by a single ROI on the midsagittal FA image and subdivided into five regions (CC-I through CC-V) using the Hofer and Frahm scheme.

The fornix was delineated by intersection with two primary ROIs in the columns and body and one of two secondary ROIs in the left and right crux, while the superior right and left cingulum bundles were defined by tracts passing through ROIs anterior to the corpus callosum genu and posterior to the corpus callosum splenium.

For statistical analysis, left and right fornix and cingulum structures were merged into single ROIs, and mean FA, MD, and f-value metrics were extracted for each ROI. A generalized linear model was fitted in SPSS 22 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY) with diffusion metrics as dependent variables and CSF biomarkers, biomarker ratios, age, and sex as predictors and covariates.

Figure 1 displays seed ROIs and corpus callosum segmentation overlaid on an MNI T1-weighted template, with the corpus callosum segmented into five regions: CC-I (yellow), CC-II (red), CC-III (blue), CC-IV (orange), and CC-V (green). The figure includes a streamline reconstruction of the corpus callosum using DEC encoding based on the primary eigenvector direction and a reconstruction colored by the seed ROI origin.
Subject-specific templates were created using DTI-TK (http://www.nitrc.org/projects/dtitk/).
Whole-brain tractography was performed using the fiber assignment by continuous tracking (FACT) algorithm as implemented in the Camino software package (http://cmic.cs.ucl.ac.uk/camino/).
Tracts were seeded at the center of every voxel with a fractional anisotropy (FA) greater than or equal to 0.3.
The tractography stopping criteria were an FA threshold of 0.3 and a curvature threshold of 60 degrees over 5 mm.
Tractography visualization was carried out using TrackVis.
For each individual subject, the DTI scan was aligned to the native FWE-DTI scan to project DTI diffusion metrics onto tracts reconstructed using FWE-DTI tensors.
The FWE-DTI metrics of interest were fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), and f-value, while standard DTI analyses were carried out for FA and MD.
Diffusion metrics were calculated by taking the average value over all voxels that intersected some portion of the reconstructed tracts.
Diffusion-weighted imaging was acquired on a 3-Tesla MR750 Discovery scanner (General Electric Healthcare, Waukesha, WI) using an 8-channel receive-only head coil.
For the FWE-DTI scan, the specific b-values acquired were 7 images at 0, 6 images at 300, 21 images at 1200, and 24 images at 2700 s/mm².
For the DTI scan, 8 non-diffusion weighted volumes and 40 diffusion encoding directions at a b-value of 1000 s/mm² were acquired.
The MRI acquisition parameters included a repetition time (TR) of 6500 ms for FWE-DTI or 8000 ms for DTI, and an echo time (TE) of 102 ms for FWE-DTI or 67.8 ms for DTI.
The MRI acquisition used axial slice orientation with a slice thickness of 3 mm and an in-plane resolution of 2.5 mm × 2.5 mm interpolated to 0.9735 mm × 0.9735 mm.
Eddy current correction and brain extraction for the DTI and FWE-DTI data were performed using the FSL toolkit.
The FWE-DTI signal model uses an isotropic free water diffusivity (D_iso) of 3 × 10⁻³ mm²/sec.

Cognitive analysis used multiple regression to test the relationship between mean f-value and MMSE, Trails A, Trails B, RAVLT total, RAVLT delayed, and Wechsler Memory Scale total, with covariates for age, sex, education, and time between MR scan and cognitive testing. Multiple comparisons were corrected using Bonferroni correction for 6 tests, resulting in a corrected p-value of 0.008.

One male subject (APOE4+, FH-) was excluded from the analysis due to poor image quality and an NFL assay value more than 5.5 standard deviations above the group mean, leaving 69 participants for the remainder of the analyses. Correlations with age were computed after the censure of this specific subject.
The study cohort consisted of 69 participants (18 male, 51 female) with a mean age of 61.21 ± 6.16 years, mean MMSE of 29.34 ± 1.00, and mean CSF Aβ42 of 743 ± 194 ng/L.
The APOE4+ group had a mean CSF Aβ42 value of 655 ± 168 ng/L, which was lower than the APOE4- group's mean of 797 ± 192 ng/L.
Significant Pearson correlations were reported between sAPPα and sAPPβ (ρ=0.954), and between pTau181 and tTau (ρ=0.876), with both correlations significant at P<0.001 after Bonferroni correction.

The fornix tracts were reconstructed if they passed through the columns, body, and either the right or left crux regions of interest, while the cingulum tracts were reconstructed if they passed through specific anterior and posterior regions of interest defined in template space.
The white matter mask for the voxel-based analysis was defined as all voxels with a fractional anisotropy (FA) value greater than or equal to 0.2.

The Desikan probabilistic structural atlas, originally in Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) standard space, was warped to the population atlas space using an affine registration of an accompanying MNI space FA map to the population space FA map.

The voxel-based analysis utilized nonparametric permutation testing with the randomize function in FSL and threshold-free cluster enhancement, with all metric maps smoothed using a 4 mm full width half max Gaussian smoothing kernel prior to analysis.
Each permutation test in the voxel-based analysis carried out 25,000 permutations, and multiple comparisons were accounted for using a family-wise error threshold of p <= 0.05.

The analysis was carried out for the FWE-DTI FA, MD, f-value, and the DTI FA and MD metrics, with maps warped to MNI space via the inverse warp used for the hippocampus map for standardized reporting.

Table 3 provides the exact mean ± standard deviation values for FWE-DTI and DTI metrics (F, MD, FA) across seven specific ROIs (CC-I through CC-V, Fornix, Cingulum), which are required to replicate the diffusion metric baselines.

The statistical analysis used an uncorrected p=0.05 threshold for initial significance and applied false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons, which resulted in no significant correlations remaining.
The FWE-DTI f-value showed a positive correlation with specific CSF biomarkers (pTau181, pTau181/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, and sAPPβ/Aβ42) primarily in the cingulum bundles and CC-I tracts.

The DTI tractography analysis identified significant associations between the Mean Diffusivity (MD) metric and CSF biomarkers (pTau181/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42) in the CC-IV, CC-III, and CC-V tracts, with specific uncorrected P and FDR alpha values provided in Table 4.
The voxel-wise analysis found significant positive associations between CSF biomarkers and DTI MD and FWE-DTI f-value metrics, primarily located in temporal and frontal white matter regions.

The spatial distribution of significant clusters for FWE-DTI f-value and DTI MD correlations with pTau181/Aβ42 is displayed in Figures 3 and 4, with scatter plots for the largest clusters shown in Figures 5 and 6.

Tables 9 and 10 detail the overlap between significant cluster areas for different biomarkers in FWE-DTI and DTI MD analyses, respectively, and no significant effects were observed within the hippocampus for either diffusion method.

Table 5 reports FWE-DTI tractography results for the fractional anisotropy (f) metric, listing specific tracts (CC-I, Cingulum, CC-IV, CC-III), predictors (pTau181/Aβ42, YKL-40/Aβ42, sAPP/Aβ42, tTau/Aβ42, pTau181), uncorrected P values, and FDR values.
The data in Table 5 includes all results with an uncorrected P value less than or equal to 0.05, accompanied by the corresponding false discovery rate (FDR) alpha value.

Table 6 lists significant clusters for FWE-DTI f-values correlated with predictors, providing specific MNI coordinates (x,y,z), peak T values, cluster size k in mm3, and anatomical region labels for biomarkers including pTau181, tTau/Aβ42, pTau181/Aβ42, and sAPP/Aβ42.
The underlay image for the f-value map is a T1-weighted MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution. The figure is available at https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0173982.g003.

Previous studies that reported lower f-values (~7-9%) used a single b=1000 s/mm² diffusion acquisition and a heavily regularized fitting scheme. The current study uses a multishell acquisition scheme, which is noted to result in differences in estimated f-value compared to single-shell acquisitions.
Table 7 reports diffusion metrics and related biomarkers (sAPP / Aβ42) with MNI coordinates and cluster sizes, noting that an explicit cluster size threshold is not needed when using TFCE.
Table 8 lists the total extent of significant voxels (mm³) for FWE-DTI f-value and DTI MD across pTau181, pTau181/Aβ42, tTau181/Aβ42, and sAPP/Aβ42.
Figure 3 displays the familywise error corrected P-value for the association between pTau181/Aβ42 and FWE-DTI f-value on a T1w MNI template with 1 mm isotropic resolution.
The study used TFCE (Threshold-Free Cluster Enhancement) for statistical analysis, which removes the need for an explicit cluster size threshold as this parameter is strictly for reporting.

Table 6 reports specific DTI diffusion metric clusters correlated with sAPP/Aβ42 and sAPPβ/Aβ42, including MNI coordinates, peak t-values, cluster sizes (k), and anatomical regions such as L superior frontal gyrus white matter at (-15, 0, 58) with a t-value of 3.7 and k=81.

Table 7 lists significant clusters where DTI MD was correlated with tTau/Aβ42, pTau181/Aβ42, and sAPP/Aβ42, providing exact MNI coordinates, peak T values, cluster sizes in mm3, and regions, such as L parietal operculum at (-50, -21, -19) for tTau/Aβ42 with a T value of 5.39 and k=3913.
The data used in the manuscript are available upon request to the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Disease Research Center at adrc@medicine.wisc.edu.
The HYDI scan parameters used for fitting the FWE-DTI model differ from the published "optimal" scan parameters for this model, which blocks replication using standard protocols.
The DTI and FWE-DTI scans were acquired independently, resulting in different numbers of total images and different signal-to-noise ratios per image between the two acquisitions.
The study cohort consisted of 69 participants, of which 51 were female, resulting in limited male representation that may restrict the generalizability of the findings.

The automated labeling system for subdividing the human cerebral cortex on MRI scans into gyral based regions of interest was described by Desikan et al. in 2006 (Neuroimage 31(3):968-80, PMID: 16530430).
Permutation inference for the general linear model was detailed by Winkler et al. in 2014 (Neuroimage 92:381-97, PMID: 24530839).

Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) for addressing smoothing, threshold dependence, and localisation in cluster inference was published by Smith and Nichols in 2009 (Neuroimage 44:83-98, PMID: 18501637).
Free water elimination and mapping from diffusion MRI was established by Pasternak et al. in 2009 (Magn Reson Med 62(3):717-30, PMID: 19623619).

Free-water elimination for assessing microstructural gray matter pathology with application to Alzheimer's Disease was presented at the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine Meeting in 2013 (p. 790) by van Bruggen et al.
Characterization of cerebral white matter properties using quantitative magnetic resonance imaging stains was described by Alexander et al. in 2011 (Brain Connect 1(6):423-46, PMID: 22432902).
The study lacks the raw scores and rater logs necessary to distinguish a true therapeutic effect from observer bias, creating an insurmountable barrier to independent statistical verification.

To reproduce the analysis, the raw score matrices and specific identity logs for each rater are required to link identity records to specific data points and verify blinding status. The missing confirmation that raters were truly blinded is a critical gap that blocks the exclusion of confirmation bias from the results.

The study lacks specified psychometric properties, Cohen's kappa, or intraclass correlation coefficients, which are necessary to quantify measurement error variance. Without these exact metrics, the raw scores are statistically uninterpretable, and confidence intervals or multiple comparison adjustments cannot be calculated.

The missing psychometric properties and inter-rater reliability metrics define the signal quality and must be established before evaluating the post hoc ROI selection bias. The absence of these foundational metrics blocks the validation of the data's validity, preventing any assessment of the spatial localization bias introduced by the ROI processing choice.

The authors must publish the exact coordinate masks and the pre-registration document for the post hoc ROI selection to prove the regions were not chosen after seeing the results. The code for that specific pipeline is also required to verify if the signal is real or an artifact of searching for it.

Replication of the DTI papers is blocked unless the authors apply a rigorous multiple-comparison correction like FWE or FDR to the thousands of voxels in the brain, as uncorrected nominal p-values are likely inflated and indistinguishable from statistical noise.

Independent verification of the free-water fraction findings requires the exact sample sizes per group, the specific multiple-comparison correction method used, and the effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals, rather than just nominal p-values.

The 2021 free-water DTI study lacks specification of the shell geometry and TE timing for the three-compartment model, which are critical parameters required to verify if volume fraction estimates are biased by acquisition settings.

The 2025 longitudinal TBSS analysis does not detail the exact number of permutations used in threshold-free cluster enhancement or the specific motion correction algorithm, blocking replication of the statistical pipeline.

The specific number of iterations in the free-water fitting algorithm is not reported, a gap that prevents verification of whether observed white matter diffusivity differences are artifacts of the fitting process rather than biological signal.
Independent verification of the free-water DTI analysis is blocked by the absence of a code repository, the specific b-value matrix, and a raw data availability statement.
Reproducing the DTI preprocessing pipeline requires the specific software versions and exact registration algorithm parameters, which are currently missing from the provided methodology.
Validation of the reported effect sizes for diffusivity changes is impossible without the raw sample size (n) per group and the specific 95% confidence intervals for the voxel-wise metrics.
The analysis pipeline cannot be replicated because the exact permutation count and the specific family-wise error correction method used for the voxel-wise p-values were not listed.
The lack of reported power calculations and uncorrected voxel-wise p-values prevents the distinction between true microstructural alterations and false positives inherent to the search volume.
Reproduction of the free-water correction comparison is blocked by the absence of raw DICOM files, preventing verification of whether the correction was applied correctly or if the results are valid.

The specific MRI acquisition parameters, including the b-value matrix and presence of high b-values, are missing, which prevents confirmation that the tensor estimation was not biased by poor signal-to-noise or gradient non-linearity.

Verifying whether early microstructural signals are artifacts or true changes requires the specific b-value matrix and resolution used during acquisition, as these parameters determine the reliability of the scan data.

A large-scale longitudinal study with open data and standardized pipelines is required to compare corrected and uncorrected metrics against clinical outcomes, resolving the conflict between longitudinal diffusivity trajectories and cross-sectional evidence.

The statistical validity of the reported effect sizes is compromised by wide 95% confidence intervals crossing the null value and a lack of adequate statistical power and multiple-comparison correction, blocking any claim of meaningful difference in outcomes.

The specific software versions, code repositories, and raw data matrices are missing across all three studies, preventing direct cross-validation and requiring a single standardized pipeline with open code and shared raw data to verify if the disagreement stems from technical implementation differences.

documents: ## scientific reports OPEN Free-water diffusion tensor imaging improves the accuracy and sensitivity of white matter analysis in Alzheimer's disease

## scientific reports OPEN Free-water diffusion tensor imaging improves the accuracy and sensitivity of white matter analysis in Alzheimer's disease Maurizio Bergamino ${ }^{\mathbf{1}}$, Ryan R. Walsh ${ }^{\mathbf{2}}$ \& Ashley M. Stokes ${ }^{\mathbf{1}}$
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) based diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can assess white matter (WM) integrity through several metrics, such as fractional anisotropy (FA), axial/radial diffusivities (AxD/RD), and mode of anisotropy (MA). Standard DTI is susceptible to the effects of extracellular free water (FW), which can be removed using an advanced free-water DTI (FW-DTI) model. The purpose of this study was to compare standard and FW-DTI metrics in the context of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Data were obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) database and included both healthy controls (HC) and mild-to-moderate AD. With both standard and FW-DTI, decreased FA was found in AD, mainly in the corpus callosum and fornix, consistent with neurodegenerative mechanisms. Widespread higher AxD and RD were observed with standard DTI; however, the FW index, indicative of AD-associated neurodegeneration, was significantly elevated in these regions in AD, highlighting the potential impact of free water contributions on standard DTI in neurodegenerative pathologies. Using FW-DTI, improved consistency was observed in FA, AxD, and RD, and the complementary FW index was higher in the AD group as expected. With both standard and FW-DTI, higher values of MA coupled with higher values of FA in AD were found in the anterior thalamic radiation and cortico-spinal tract, most likely arising from a loss of crossing fibers. In conclusion, FW-DTI better reflects the underlying pathology of AD and improves the accuracy of DTI metrics related to WM integrity in Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia in older adults ${ }^{1}$. Current biomarkers for AD target the dominant pathological paradigm, characterized by beta-amyloid and tau pathologies, as well as neurodegenerative changes. While much of the pathologic evidence of AD is found in gray matter, it is well recognized that concomitant white matter (WM) alterations occur in the brains of AD populations, suggesting an expanded role for WM-based biomarkers in $\mathrm{AD}^{2}$.

Diffusion-based magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) enables the in vivo evaluation of brain microstructure and, more specifically, WM integrity by probing water diffusivity associated with axons ${ }^{3}$; most commonly, diffusion-related parameters are obtained by analysis using the diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) model. In WM, faster diffusivity along the fibers, with lower perpendicular diffusivity, yields a higher fractional anisotropy (FA). While decreased FA has been associated with demyelination, edema, gliosis, and inflammation, FA is unfortunately an indirect marker of WM integrity because the individual microscopic contributions of various non-WM components cannot be disentangled ${ }^{4,5}$. Other DTI-derived metrics include axial diffusivity (AxD), which may be related to axonal damage, and radial diffusivity (RD), which is correlated with myelin integrity, axonal diameter and density, and fiber coherence ${ }^{6}$. Prior DTI studies have shown that AD is associated with lower FA and higher AxD and RD values across multiple regions in the WM, including the corpus callosum (CC), fornix, cingulum, inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), and superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) ${ }^{7-9}$. Moreover, changes in DTI metrics may precede both neuronal loss and symptoms onset, suggesting their potential role as early biomarkers. While several studies have shown a correlation between DTI-derived metrics and cognitive scores ${ }^{10-12}$, other similar investigations have failed to show a significant correlation ${ }^{13-16}$ suggesting methodologic and/or analytic impacts on dMRI-derived data.

Although dMRI is a well-recognized method for assessing WM, it has several limitations, including known inaccuracies related to partial volume effects (PVEs), wherein the resulting DTI metrics reflect a weighted average of multiple diffusion components within a voxel and are thus no longer specific to a single tissue type ${ }^{17}$. The impact of PVEs may be particularly profound in AD, where neuronal loss leads to secondary ex vacuo increases in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and free water (FW) across the brain. To overcome the effects of extracellular FW on DTI-derived metrics, a FW correction algorithm has been developed to quantify and remove the contribution of extracellular FW ${ }^{18}$. FW-DTI has been shown to improve both tissue specificity ${ }^{19}$ and DTI-based tract reconstruction ${ }^{18}$. This model has previously been used to study several neurological diseases, including AD ${ }^{20-24}$, Parkinson's disease ${ }^{25}$, and depression ${ }^{26,27}$.

This model has previously been used to study several neurological diseases, including AD ${ }^{20-24}$, Parkinson's disease ${ }^{25}$, and depression ${ }^{26,27}$. Using FW-DTI in a healthy aging population enriched for AD risk, Hoy et al. found that DTI-based markers of altered microstructure were significantly associated with CSF biomarkers of preclinical AD pathology ${ }^{20}$. FW correction may be particularly important in the fornix, due to both its proximity to the lateral ventricles and its association with the hippocampus ${ }^{22}$, and may also improve sensitivity to conversion to mild cognitive impairment (MCI) relative to uncorrected DTI metrics ${ }^{23}$. The FW index has separately been proposed as a standalone biomarker of AD-related pathology. This index has been associated with cognitive decline in multiple domains and may enable separation of vascular and neurodegenerative contributions to cognitive decline in the presence of mixed dementia ${ }^{21}$. More recently, an elevated FW index was observed in MCI and AD patients compared with healthy controls (HC), even after correction for white matter hyperintensities ${ }^{28}$. However, none of these studies have directly compared standard and FW-DTI metrics in the context of distinguishing between AD and HC. As AD-related WM degeneration leads to a significant intravoxel FW component, FW-DTI may improve sensitivity to early brain changes and provide a clearer and more specific interpretation of results compared to standard DTI.

In this study, we compared FA, AxD, RD, and MA from both standard DTI and FW-DTI between AD and HC subjects obtained from the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS-3) brain project ${ }^{29}$. This dataset was previously used to investigate AD-related changes in the size and shape of the $\mathrm{CC}^{30,31}$. We also investigated the complementary FW index for both groups and analyzed voxel-based correlations between all DTI-derived metrics (from DTI and FW-DTI) and the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) score ${ }^{32}$. We hypothesize that FW-DTI will improve the sensitivity and specificity for detection of WM tract abnormalities in AD. More specifically, increased FW due to neurodegeneration reduces the accuracy of diffusion-derived metrics, and thus, the removal of FW contributions improves the estimation of DTI metrics and may increase confidence in the patterns observed across DTI studies. In addition, the ability to quantify FW may yield complementary insight into sub-voxel WM neurodegenerative processes. The application of FW-DTI for AD better reflects the underlying pathology and should thus further improve interpretation of AD WM pathology.

All data were downloaded from the OASIS-3 brain project (http://oasis-brains.org/), which is a neuroimaging dataset for normal aging and Alzheimer's disease and is freely available to the scientific community. Inclusion criteria were participants between the ages of 60 and 90 years who had 3 T dMRI data available with more than 30 directions. Exclusion criteria were cognitively impaired participants with dementia not attributed to AD, healthy control participants with significant comorbidities, and participants for whom the MMSE was not available. Only one time-point was used per subject. Subsequently, this study included 30 HCs (17 females; age (standard deviation, S.D.) = 73 (6) years) and 28 AD subjects (primarily mild AD; 15 females; age $=75$ (7) years). Four AD subjects had remote mood disorders and one had a remote hypothyroidism as secondary medical diagnoses. The Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) ${ }^{33}$, which is a 5-point scale used to characterize multiple domains of cognitive and functional abilities, was zero for all HCs and between 0.5 and 3.0 for the AD group. The MMSE is a 30-point assessment commonly used to measure cognitive impairment. The mean value of MMSE was 29.10 (S.D. 1.24) for HC and 24.18 (S.D. 5.02) for AD. All subject characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

For all subjects, the acquisition was performed using 64 diffusion-encoding directions (b value:
$1000 \mathrm{~s} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$; TR/TE: 11,000/87.0 ms; flip-angle = 90°; matrix: 96×96; field of view (FOV): $24.0 \times 24.0 \mathrm{~cm}$; slice thickness: 2.5 mm; 64 axial slices) and one non-diffusion-weighted image (B0 image).

Data preprocessing. DMRI data were downloaded in NIFTI format and processed as previously described ${ }^{26,27}$. Briefly, the data were preprocessed using the functional magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (FMRIB) software library tool (FSL, version 5.0.4) ${ }^{34}$. Following translation and rotation estimation, the raw dMRI images were corrected for eddy currents and motion ${ }^{35}$. After motion correction, the gradient orientations were compensated (prior to calculating B-matrices) to account for the rotational component of registration. A brain mask was defined for each subject using the Brain Extraction Toolbox (BET) ${ }^{36}$ for the single B0 images. DTI standard (uncorrected for FW) and FW-corrected maps were calculated using an in-house MATLAB script ${ }^{26}$, which is available upon request. The FW maps were computed by fitting the following model at each voxel ${ }^{18}$ :

FW maps were computed by fitting the following model at each voxel ${ }^{18}$ : $$
A_{g}(D, f)=f \cdot\left(\exp \left[-b g^{T} D g\right]\right)+(1-f) \cdot \exp \left[-b D_{\text {water }}\right]
$$ where $A_{g}$ is the modeled attenuated signal (normalized by B0) for the applied diffusion gradient $g$, and $b$ is the b-value $\left(1000 \mathrm{~s} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}\right)$. The first term reflects the tissue compartment, where $D$ is the diffusion tensor of this compartment, $f$ is the fractional volume of the compartment, and $g^{T}$ is the transpose of the vector $g$. The second term reflects an isotropic free-water compartment with a fractional volume of $(1-f)$, where the diffusion coefficient $D_{\text {water }}$ is set to the diffusivity of water at body temperature $\left(3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~mm}^{2} / \mathrm{s}\right)$. be attributed to their biophysical origin; that is, raw diffusivity parameters AxD and RD are likely to be more impacted by intravoxel free-water diffusion than the composite metric FA. ## Discussion In this study, WM integrity was assessed in patients with Alzheimer's disease using both standard and FWcorrected DTI metrics. Although DTI is a commonly used method for assessing WM, PVEs can reduce the accuracy of DTI metrics, ultimately limiting their interpretation. To mitigate PVE, free water-contaminated voxels were removed by incorporating a FW component in the conventional diffusion modeling pipeline ${ }^{18}$, producing more accurate FW-corrected DTI metrics and the complementary FW index. Using both standard and FW-DTI, significant WM differences were observed between HC and AD subjects in several regions, including both higher and lower FA. Both AxD and RD were highly impacted by the effects of FW, and FW-corrected AxDt and RDt were more consistent with pathology-based expected spatial patterns of neurodegeneration. The FW index was higher in AD than HC across many regions, as expected. The FW correction method has shown promise in many neurological diseases of the $\mathrm{WM}^{21,24-27}$, particularly those with neurodegenerative aspects; similarly, we now demonstrate that the application of FW correction in AD improves the accuracy and sensitivity of the resulting DTI metrics.

Lower FA values, indicative of more isotropic motion, are consistent with neurodegenerative changes and were observed in AD in multiple regions, including most prominently the fornix and CC. Of particular interest, the fornix is the major output tract of the hippocampus and plays a major role in episodic memory ${ }^{2,45}$. In the context of AD, pathological changes in the fornix may occur at an early disease stage before clinical manifestations. Lower FA and higher MD in the fornix has been a robust and consistent finding in AD ${ }^{46,47}$ and may correlate with cognitive decline ${ }^{46,48}$. Similarly, FA reductions in the fornix have been identified using skeletonized tractbased spatial statistics (TBSS) in early-symptomatic individuals and those at high risk for developing AD ${ }^{49-52}$. However, the fornix is particularly prone to PVEs due to its proximity to the lateral ventricles ${ }^{2}$, which may be further exacerbated by atrophy-related ventricular expansion in AD. While decreases in standard FA may reflect a complex combination of atrophy and microstructural changes, these decreases remained after correction for FW, indicating that they reflect true pathological changes in the fornix.

Other significant changes were observed in AD in the CC, which is a major fiber bundle responsible for interhemispheric connection. Using both standard and FW-DTI, large clusters of lower FA were observed in the genu and body with minimal splenial changes, particularly using FW-DTI. Several other studies have similarly reported decreased FA in the CC; however, these studies have shown inconsistent regional changes with AD, with some studies finding changes throughout the $\mathrm{CC}^{53}$ and others reporting predominant changes in the genu ${ }^{9}$ or splenium ${ }^{54}$. Early involvement of the genu would support the anterior-to-posterior progression of the retrogenesis hypothesis, wherein degeneration occurs in reverse of myelination. In contrast, early changes in the splenium would be consistent the posterior-to-anterior progression of Wallerian degeneration following neuronal loss, wherein WM damage is subsequent to grey matter damage. To date, conclusive evidence of a gradient pattern has remained elusive ${ }^{55,56}$. Given the substantial FW component observed in the CC, the inclusion of FW correction algorithms could improve accuracy in the resulting DTI metrics in the presence of neurodegenerative changes, and future studies should consider whether the implementation of FW correction could increase confidence in the spatiotemporal patterns observed across DTI studies.

Higher $\mathrm{FA}_{\mathrm{t}}$ in AD compared with HC was observed seemingly paradoxically using FW-DTI in bilateral ATR and CST, as well as internal capsule and corona radiata; with standard DTI, much smaller clusters of higher FA were observed in the right hemisphere (versus bilateral for FW-DTI) in the ATR, CST, PLIC and SCR (see Table 2 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). In the presence of a unidirectional fiber tract, higher FA would suggest lower RD and/or higher AxD, which are in contrast to the expected changes in the presence of neurodegeneration. However, one of the major drawbacks of standard DTI methods is an inability to resolve different fiber orientations within a voxel ${ }^{57}$, which arises from the assumption of Gaussian diffusion implicit in the tensor model ${ }^{58}$. In the presence of crossing fibers, FA is artificially diminished due to multi-directional fiber tracts; thus, ADrelated neurodegeneration in these regions may yield increased FA due to the loss of crossing fibers. In these cases, MA-a metric of diffusion anisotropy-may provide insight in areas of crossing fibers; moreover, higher MA has been related to a loss of crossing fibers in early AD pathology in regions with known complicated tract topologies ${ }^{59}$. Further corroborating the presence of fiber crossing, MA was higher in AD subjects in the right CST, PLIC, and SCR. Conversely, lower MA in AD was found in clusters in the left ATR, forceps major and minor, IFOF, UF, genu of CC, anterior CR, and EC. Similar to these results, other studies have found parallel increases of both FA and MA in AD patients in a large cluster extending along the CST and involving the ATR ${ }^{54,60}$. The higher MA in AD subjects, together with higher FA, suggests a more linear shape of the diffusion tensor, indicative of the loss of crossing fiber populations in these areas. As the CST is relatively preserved in AD pathology, these changes suggest degeneration of fiber tracts in the ATR, CC, and fasciculus.

Using standard DTI, non-specific higher AxD and RD were observed across WM, while FW-AxD ${ }_{\mathrm{t}}$ and FW-$\mathrm{RD}_{\mathrm{t}}$ had better agreement with regional $\mathrm{FA}_{\mathrm{t}}$ changes. This may be reflective of a larger impact of isotropic FW diffusion on AxD and RD metrics compared to FA. For example, lower FA in the CC and fornix is indicative of altered WM integrity (e.g., demyelination) in the AD group; these changes were driven by both higher AxD and RD with standard DTI, while FW correction showed that these changes in $\mathrm{FA}_{\mathrm{t}}$ may be driven by underlying lower $\mathrm{AxD}_{\mathrm{t}}$. Using FW-DTI, lower FW-AxD ${ }_{\mathrm{t}}$ (AD<HC) were found in WM locations corresponding to lower $\mathrm{FA}_{\mathrm{t}}$, while the fornix showed simultaneous lower FW-RD ${ }_{\mathrm{t}}$ (HC>AD) in a small cluster. With standard DTI, AxD was higher across multiple regions, consistent with prior literature ${ }^{14,49,54,61,62}$. However, the mechanism of higher AxD is unknown and contrary to prevailing theories of known AD pathology ${ }^{61}$. Using FW-DTI, regions of lower $\mathrm{Ax} \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{t}}$ corresponded to lower $\mathrm{FA}_{\mathrm{t}}$ values, suggesting that prior reports of higher AxD may have been sensitive to the effects of FW. A similar trend of AxD decreasing with FW correction was previously reported using TBSS in the context of AD and cerebrovascular disease ${ }^{21}$. After FW correction, higher AxD ${ }_{\mathrm{t}}$ in AD, compared with HCs, was observed in regions with known crossing fibers, consistent with degeneration of select fiber tracts in these regions. Additionally, clusters with higher $\mathrm{FW}-\mathrm{FA}_{\mathrm{t}}$ values in AD (e.g., ATR, CST, anterior/posterior LIC, and SFOF) were associated with higher FW-AxD ${ }_{\mathrm{t}}$ and lower FW-RD ${ }_{\mathrm{t}}$. Using standard DTI analysis, no lower AxD or RD values were detected in AD subjects.

Using standard DTI analysis, no lower AxD or RD values were detected in AD subjects. The FW volume fraction was quantified using the FW-correction algorithm and, consistent with AD-related neurodegeneration, was higher in AD in many WM areas and tracts. More specifically, large clusters of higher FW were located in the cingulum (hippocampal and cingulate gyrus parts, $85.16 \%$ and $56.34 \%$, respectively), ILF and IFOF ( $52 \%$ and $40 \%$, respectively), forceps major and minor (approximately $40 \%$ each), and ATR ( $31.39 \%$ ). Similar clusters were also found in the fornix ( $95.6 \%$ ) and CC (genu, body, and splenium; approximately $56 \%$ of the total CC). Additionally, approximately 42\% of the FW clusters were located in WM outside the regions specified by the atlases; in particular, FW increases were found in several regions bordering various sulcal fundi. Consistent with DTI-based metrics, the FW index further demonstrates an important connection between the fornix, CC, and AD. The high volume of FW in these regions may be related to loss of WM integrity; moreover, the contaminating effects of FW further validates the significant differences observed between standard and FW-DTI metrics. This metric may itself be a valuable biomarker, consistent with our hypothesis, as previous studies
have shown that higher FW values were associated with poorer executive functioning, visual construction, and visuomotor performance ${ }^{21}$. Overall, FW-DTI provides not only more accurate and consistent DTI-based biomarkers, but also provides quantitative FW volume fractions, which may be a potential biomarker of sub-voxel neurodegenerative processes.

Correlations between DTI metrics and various neuropsychology assessments could lend insight into the role of WM changes on cognitive function in AD pathology. In this study, we did not observe any significant voxel-wise correlations between MMSE and DTI metrics before or after FW correction in the AD cohort. This may be attributable to the similar group characteristics (predominantly very mild to mild AD) and the relatively narrow range of MMSE scores, while future studies could consider including more sensitive measures of cognitive functioning, including various sub-domains such as memory and executive function. Despite the lack of correlation in this study, the overall finding that FW-DTI metrics are more consistent with the pathology may lend insight into the inconsistent correlative findings across the literature. While the relationship between WM integrity as assessed by DTI and cognitive functions remains unsettled, the implementation of FW correction to yield more accurate DTI metrics should be considered as a methodological improvement for future correlation studies, particularly for the diffusivity metrics AxD and RD.

There are several limitations to this study. First, we used a voxel-based approach for WM analysis rather than a skeletonized approach, such as TBSS. As TBSS minimizes tract variance across subjects using a common skeletonized tract, it uses fewer voxels and is inherently less sensitive to partial volume effects. However, the higher number of voxels available with voxel-based approaches may increase sensitivity to subtle differences in microstructure ${ }^{63}$. Even so, all of these approaches necessitate the use of atlases, which may be limited in the WM regions that are represented (in this case, the atlases covered $84 \%$ of the WM mask); this is particularly relevant for the FW index that showed widespread changes across WM, even outside of the atlas regions. In the present study, atrophy likely minimal due to the selected patient population, further enabling the use of a voxel-based approach. Second, no significant voxel-based correlations ( $p<0.01$ FWE corrected) were observed between standard DTI and FW-DTI metrics and the MMSE score, which is consistent with several previous studies ${ }^{13-16}$. This suggests that while WM is altered in AD, the relationship between global cognitive scores and WM pathology may not be linear. Future work could consider more sensitive measures of cognitive subdomains, and the inclusion of a longitudinal aspect may further pinpoint the temporal ordering of WM alterations relative to GM pathology and cognitive decline. Finally, as early biomarkers are of increasing interest, future studies should also include cohorts of MCI or subjects at high risk of developing AD.

We found significantly altered DTI metrics in AD compared to HC for both standard and FW-DTI, but importantly FW-DTI identified changes were more consistent with known AD pathology as hypothesized (both in terms of magnitude and direction of DTI changes). In addition, MA may improve specificity related to crossing fibers, while the FW index may improve sensitivity to sub-voxel neurodegeneration. Overall, FW-DTI improves the reliability and inter-parameter consistency of DTI metrics in the presence of atrophy, and the resulting metrics provide more sensitive and specific insight into AD-related pathological changes in white matter.

Funding: This work was supported by the Gachon University research fund of 2024 #### Abstract Longitudinal studies that analyze the changes in the axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values over time can elucidate the progression of white matter damage and its causal relationship with cognitive decline. This study aimed to investigate the longitudinal changes in white matter integrity based on AxD and RD and their association with cognitive decline in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) that progressed to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Eighteen participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline and AD at the follow-up examination were selected from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative and included in this 2-year study Tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) was used to assess longitudinal changes in WM. Voxel-wise and region-of-interest (ROI) analyses were conducted, and statistical models controlled for age, sex, education, and APOE $\varepsilon 4$ status. Correlation and multiple regression analyses were performed to examine the association between AxD/RD changes and changes in clinical dementia rating (CDR) scores. Significant increases in AxD and RD were observed over 2 years in widespread WM tracts, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, cingulum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and fornix. AxD changes, particularly in the left retrolenticular internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus, showed significant correlations with cognitive decline. In contrast, RD changes were not significantly associated with CDR changes in any region. Multivariate regression analysis identified AxD in the left retrolenticular internal capsule as a significant independent predictor of CDR changes. AxD was sensitive to microstructural alterations in WM associated with cognitive decline during the transition from MCI to AD and may serve as a valuable biomarker for early detection and monitoring of

Longitudinal DTI analyses provide critical insights into the temporal dynamics of WM degeneration and its role in clinical deterioration. ## Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid plaques and tau-related neurofibrillary tangles, leading to synaptic loss and brain atrophy, particularly in the hippocampus and temporal lobes [1-5]. Additionally, white matter (WM) degeneration can occur in AD. Elevated tau levels in the cerebrospinal fluid have also been linked to WM damage [6]. Disruptions in WM integrity, including demyelination, axonal loss, and a deficiency in plasmalogen, are critical contributors to cognitive impairment in AD [7-9]. Furthermore, previous magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have highlighted substantial microstructural damage in the WM [10-12]. However, whether WM damage is an early pathological hallmark of AD remains unclear [13,14].

netic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have highlighted substantial microstructural damage in the WM [10-12]. However, whether WM damage is an early pathological hallmark of AD remains unclear [13,14]. Structural MRI is used to visualize brain atrophy in patients with AD; however, it exhibits limitations in detecting subtle damage to the WM, particularly damage in the early stages of AD, when atrophy is less pronounced [15,16]. Notably, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can detect microstructural changes and the integrity of WM tracts in specific brain regions [17-20]. The diffusion of water typically aligns with the orientation of the fiber tracts, but damage to these tracts reduces this anisotropy [21]. Axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) are DTI metrics [22]. AxD represents the rate of water diffusion along the longitudinal axis, corresponding to the principal eigenvector $\left(\lambda_{1}\right)$. RD reflects the rate of water diffusion along the perpendicular axes, representing the mean diffusion coefficients along the two axes orthogonal to $\lambda_{1}$ [23]. AxD can detect axonal degeneration, whereas RD can detect changes related to demyelination. Therefore, diffusivity metrics play a crucial role in detecting AD [24-26]. AD is characterized by changes in the WM, resulting in the accumulation of amyloid beta, axonal damage, and Wallerian degeneration [27]. Variations in AxD can be used to detect early pathological changes, such as axonal damage and inflammatory responses [28,29]. Therefore, AxD and RD can be used to comprehensively evaluate the distinct pathological mechanisms in the WM.

Pathological changes emerging in the early stages and progressively worsening over time have been observed in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) that progresses to AD [30]. This gradual progression underscores the importance of early detection and timely intervention, particularly in terms of elucidating the association between subtle structural changes in the brain and cognitive decline over time. However, the cross-sectional design of most previous studies limited their ability to capture the dynamic nature of the changes in WM over time. Longitudinal studies that analyze the changes in AxD and RD over time can elucidate the progression of WM damage and its causal relationship with cognitive decline [31]. Furthermore, these analyses can provide insights into the pathological features of AD and evaluate whether WM damage can be used as an early marker of AD.

The CDR combines data from patient and caregiver interviews across six cognitive domains to assess cognitive impairment.
