The primary eigenvalue $\left(\lambda_{1}\right)$ was used to determine the AxD, whereas the secondary eigenvalues ( $\lambda_{2}$ and $\lambda_{3}$ ) were averaged to derive the RD. ## TBSS TBSS is an automated analysis method used to evaluate the changes in fractional anisotropy (FA) in the cerebral WM. It employs voxel-wise statistics on diffusion indices while utilizing conventional voxel-based analysis techniques [33]. TBSS was selected for its robustness in aligning white matter tracts across participants and its suitability for small longitudinal datasets. It enables voxel-wise statistical analysis while minimizing the impact of spatial misregistration. However, one limitation of TBSS is that it restricts the analysis to the central white matter skeleton, potentially over-looking peripheral or crossing fiber regions where early pathological changes may also occur [34]. Future studies may benefit from complementary approaches such as fixel-based analysis or tractometry to capture a broader range of white matter alterations. Voxel-wise analysis of FA data derived from DTI images was conducted using TBSS as a preliminary step for analyzing AxD and RD. Although FA is a widely used metric in TBSS and was used in this study to construct the white matter skeleton, we did not include FA in the correlation or regression analyses. This is because FA reflects a composite of axial and radial diffusivity and may lack specificity in isolating pathological mechanisms [35]. Therefore, we focused our analyses on AxD and RD to better elucidate the distinct microstructural changes occurring in AD. The FSL was used to register the FA maps to an FA template space (FMRIB58_FA $1 \times 1 \times 1 \mathrm{~mm}$ ), created using the FA maps of the 18 participants in this study. A mean FA skeleton representing the core of the WM tracts shared among the participants was constructed by averaging the FA maps. A threshold of 0.2 was applied to refine the skeleton such that only voxels with sufficient FA values, indicating WM integrity, were included in the analysis. The normalized FA data of each participant were mapped onto this skeleton to facilitate the voxel-wise statistical analysis of cross-subject differences using general linear modeling [36]. The same skeleton and registration parameters were applied to the AxD and RD maps to ensure that these metrics were evaluated within the same structural framework. The Johns Hopkins University white-matter tractography atlas was used to conduct the region-of-interest (ROI) analysis. ROI masks were applied to the corresponding key WM tracts, including the cingulum (CG), corpus callosum (CC), and uncinate fasciculus, to extract the AxD and RD values [37]. ROI analyses were conducted in an exploratory manner based on regions that showed significant differences in AxD and RD in the TBSS whole-brain analysis. Therefore, the ROI-level statistical

Longitudinal differences in the AxD and RD values across the WM tracts were analyzed using TBSS with permutation-based statistical testing. TBSS is a voxel-wise statistical technique to improve WM skeleton alignment by applying nonparametric permutation testing to evaluate group variations and avoid arbitrary spatial smoothing. In this study, permutation testing with 5,000 iterations generated a null distribution of t-values by randomly rearranging the data among the participants [39]. Statistical significance was ascertained by matching the observed t-values to the null distribution and comparing them to a preset threshold. A threshold-free cluster enhancement method was applied within the permutation-based paired t-tests to correct for multiple comparisons at the voxel level. Statistical significance was set at $P<0.05$ and evaluated using threshold-free cluster enhancement-corrected $P$-values [40]. S2 Table summarizes the results of regression analysis for all ROIs. ## Discussion Anisotropic diffusion metrics measured using DTI, such as AxD and RD, are sensitive to microstructural barriers and obstacles (e.g., cell membranes, myelin sheaths, and microtubules) [44]. These metrics are widely recognized as indicators of WM integrity, reflecting WM damage [45]. Therefore, the changes in the WM microstructure were longitudinally evaluated by analyzing the diffusion metrics-AxD and RD. Furthermore, their associations with cognitive decline were also assessed. TBSS analysis revealed a significant increase in AxD and RD in several WM regions, such as the CC, CR, and SLF. The increase in AxD was widespread, and it correlated with cognitive decline. Conversely, RD changes across all examined WM regions did not significantly associate with CDR changes. These findings indicated that an increase in AxD is closely related to cognitive decline.

These findings indicated that an increase in AxD is closely related to cognitive decline. TBSS analysis revealed significant changes in AxD and RD across the CC, CR, CG, SLF, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF), and IC. The CC, the main WM tract connecting the left and right hemispheres of the brain, plays a critical role in maintaining cognitive function [46]. It enables efficient transmission and coordination of information between the two hemispheres, thereby facilitating the development and maintenance of cognitive abilities [47]. Particularly, the CC enables smooth communication between the hemispheres by transmitting electrical and chemical signals, thereby playing an essential role in attention, memory, language processing, spatial perception, and emotional regulation [48]. Consequently, damage to the CC can weaken the connection between the hemispheres, thereby impairing memory, attention, language processing, and other cognitive functions [49]. The CR, a part of the limbic-thalamocortical circuitry, is a vital pathway that connects the cerebral cortex with the subcortical structures. The CR facilitates communication and information exchange essential for cognitive functions, such as memory and language processing [48]. It supports sensory, motor, and cognitive control. Changes in its integrity, particularly in the ACR, can impair prefrontal cortex functions involved in cognitive control [50]. Damage to the CG, a critical component of the limbic system, is often observed in patients with AD, along with an increase in RD in the CG, indicating disruption of WM integrity [51]. These changes may disrupt connections between brain regions within the limbic system, affecting emotion regulation, memory, and cognitive processes [51,52]. The SLF, which connects the prefrontal, temporal, and occipital cortices through the posterior parietal cortex, features extensive bidirectional pathways [53]. It plays a critical role in maintaining motor coordination and gait function [54]. Therefore, damage to the SLF can impair the motor coordination system, leading to difficulties in walking and balance [55]. The IFOF links the frontal, temporal, and occipital lobes, thereby enabling the integration of auditory and visual information and contributing to higher-order cognitive processing [56]. Disruption of the IFOF can impair multisensory integration and complex cognitive functions [57]. The IC, a bilateral WM structure located in the inferomedial region of each hemisphere, carries afferent and efferent fibers to and from the cerebral cortex [58]. Notably, the posterior limb of the IC contains fiber pathways involved in language and cognitive functions [48]. Therefore, changes in the IC can result in extensive impairments in motor and sensory functions, in addition to deficits in language execution and cognitive processing [59]. These findings highlight the vulnerability of WM tracts to AD and suggest that damage to these tracts may lead to cognitive and functional impairments.

Previous cross-sectional studies have reported an increase in AxD and RD in the CC, SLF, and CG in patients with AD [60]. A longitudinal analysis of the progression from MCI to AD further demonstrated significant increases in AxD and RD in these regions, highlighting structural changes in the WM during disease progression. Diffusivity changes have also been observed in limbic system regions closely associated with lower cognitive scores, including the posterior CG, fornix, and CCS [61-64]. Notably, previous studies have reported significant correlations between cognitive scores, such as the Mini-Mental State Examination, and diffusivity changes in the posterior CG [65,66].

In the present study, AxD changes in the left retrolenticular region of the IC, left PCR, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right SLF exhibited significant correlations with changes in CDR scores, indicating that axonal degeneration in these regions may contribute to cognitive decline. The involvement of the left retrolenticular region of the IC and left PCR, which are closely connected to the temporal lobe and posterior temporoparietal circuitry, is consistent with previous research
highlighting the role of these pathways in cognitive processing and memory function [67-69]. The fornix, a major component of the limbic system, has also been widely associated with memory impairment and AD-related neurodegeneration [70]. Moreover, the SLF plays a crucial role in long-range cortical communication and has been implicated in executive function and visuospatial deficits in AD [71].

Moreover, the SLF plays a crucial role in long-range cortical communication and has been implicated in executive function and visuospatial deficits in AD [71]. Interestingly, no significant correlations were observed between RD changes and CDR changes across any of the examined WM regions in the present study. One possible explanation is that axonal degeneration, rather than myelin integrity loss, plays a predominant role in clinical progression at this stage of the disease. Increases in AxD may primarily reflect severe tissue loss, widespread structural damage, and increased extracellular space, rather than direct demyelination [72]. The observed AxD increases may reflect Wallerian degeneration, leading to progressive axonal atrophy [73,74]. Axonal loss and inflammatory responses, particularly microglial activation, have been proposed as key mechanisms underlying the pathological progression of AD, potentially explaining the strong association between AxD changes and cognitive decline in the present study [26,74]. Furthermore, AxD changes emerge earlier than RD changes during AD development [26,75]. In contrast, RD primarily reflects myelin degeneration, which may become more apparent in the later stages of AD progression. The lack of significant RD-CDR associations in this study may therefore be attributed to the temporal dynamics of pathology, with demyelination following earlier axonal damage. Additionally, technical limitations such as the spatial resolution of DTI and the skeleton-based nature of TBSS may hinder the detection of subtle peripheral WM changes where myelin loss typically occurs. Previous studies have reported mixed findings regarding RD changes in AD, with some suggesting that RD alterations are less pronounced than AxD in early stages [76], while others reported associations primarily in advanced disease [45]. These considerations underscore the importance of multimodal and longitudinal approaches to better disentangle the distinct pathological signatures captured by different DTI metrics. Therefore, AxD could be a sensitive indicator of early pathological changes. In this study, the changes in AxD exhibited a significant correlation with the changes in CDR in regions, including the left retrolenticular region of the IC, left PCR, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right SLF.

Our findings suggest that AxD changes, particularly in the left retrolenticular IC, serve as independent predictors of cognitive decline, reinforcing the hypothesis that axonal damage is the primary driver of microstructural alterations in AD progression. The significant association between AxD changes in this region and CDR reduction emphasizes the importance of axonal integrity in preserving cognitive function. These findings further imply that although axonal degeneration is clearly linked to cognitive decline, not all WM tracts equally contribute to disease progression, and regional specialization is essential in AD-related pathology. In contrast, the changes in RD across all examined WM regions were not substantially associated with CDR changes. RD is primarily associated with myelin damage; therefore, myelin loss in AD may contribute to cognitive decline by disrupting WM integrity, but it may not be the primary driver of disease progression. AxD reflects axonal pathology, and RD captures myelin-related abnormalities. Consequently, the correlation between AxD and RD observed in particular regions with cognitive decline suggests that both diffusion metrics are sensitive indicators of pathological progression [63]. While changes in AxD reflect early pathological progression, changes in RD become more prominent in the later stages of the disease progression. Therefore, AxD may be a reliable marker for identifying and monitoring the initial progression of AD, particularly given its independent association with cognitive decline observed in the present study [26,67,74].

The progression from MCI to AD was longitudinally analyzed in the present study, and the microstructural changes in WM integrity were evaluated to assess subtle pathological changes in the WM. In contrast to previous cross-sectional studies that revealed pathological changes at a specific time point, longitudinal studies, such as the present study, provide
a clearer understanding of the temporal progression of these changes and their association with cognitive decline. Therefore, AxD, which offers important insights into the underlying pathology of AD, may be a valuable biomarker for early diagnosis and tracking of disease progression. Although AxD demonstrates potential as an early biomarker of axonal degeneration in AD, its clinical translation requires further work. Specifically, standardization across imaging protocols and scanners is necessary to ensure reproducibility. In addition, normative datasets should be established to define AxD thresholds indicative of pathological changes. Future studies should also assess the cost-effectiveness and clinical utility of incorporating AxD metrics into routine diagnostic workflows.

This study has some limitations. First, changes in AxD values have been inconsistently reported across studies, with both increases and decreases being observed. This inconsistency may be attributed to multiple pathological processes, including axonal damage, inflammatory responses, and changes in the extracellular space, affecting AxD. Therefore, further studies are warranted to clarify the extent to which AxD reflects specific pathological processes. Second, although AxD and RD reflect axonal damage and myelin degeneration, respectively, they rely on simplified assumptions of the diffusion tensor model. Therefore, the complexity of actual WM structures may not be captured completely. Advanced techniques, such as neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging or multi-shell DTI, must be used in future studies to overcome these limitations. Third, the TBSS analysis in this study only focused on the core regions of the WM tract, projecting the highest FA values onto the alignment-invariant tract representation (the FA skeleton) for statistical analysis. This approach improves the precision of the analysis; however, subtle changes occurring outside the skeleton may have been overlooked. Therefore, these findings may not fully represent all structural changes in the WM. Fourth, cognitive function was evaluated using CDR scores only. CDR is a useful tool for assessing the severity of AD; however, it lacks a detailed assessment of various cognitive domains. Additional neuropsychological tools, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment or Mini-Mental State Examination, must be incorporated in future studies to comprehensively assess multidimensional cognitive changes. Fifth, the small sample size $(\mathrm{n}=18)$ limits the generalizability of the findings, as a small sample size reduces the statistical power and increases the likelihood of overlooking subtle changes. Therefore, future studies with larger sample sizes must be conducted to validate these findings and improve their reliability. Additionally, although uncorrected p-values were reported due to the small sample size, we acknowledge the risk of inflated falsepositive rates. Therefore, future studies should validate our findings in larger samples using more stringent correction methods such as False Discovery Rate. Additionally, ROI analyses were conducted post hoc based on TBSS findings, which may raise concerns about circular reasoning. Although these exploratory analyses provided further insights into regional associations with cognitive decline, future studies should employ a priori ROI definitions or independent datasets for validation to enhance the robustness of the findings. Another limitation of this study is the exclusive use of the CDR as a cognitive measure. While CDR is a valid instrument for staging the severity of dementia, it does not capture domain-specific cognitive deficits. Future studies should incorporate neuropsychological batteries that assess memory, language, attention, and executive function to more precisely elucidate the relationship between white matter microstructural changes and cognitive decline. Lastly, although APOE $\varepsilon 4$ status was included as a covariate in all statistical models, potential interaction effects between $\varepsilon 4$ status and white matter changes were not tested in this study. Due to the limited sample size and small number of $\varepsilon 4$ carriers, such analyses may have been underpowered. Further studies with larger samples should explore whether APOE $\varepsilon 4$ status moderates the relationship between DTI metrics and cognitive decline.

The findings of the present study demonstrate that an increase in AxD is particularly prevalent and strongly associated with changes in cognitive status. Therefore, AxD may be a sensitive indicator of early pathological changes. Furthermore, an increase in RD was observed in fewer regions. Collectively, the findings of the present study highlight the utility of AxD as a potential biomarker for the early detection and monitoring of AD progression, providing insights into the distinct role of WM diffusion metrics reflecting axonal and myelin pathology.

*Andrew.Hoy@usuhs.edu #### Abstract Brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) begin decades before disease diagnosis. While $\beta$-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are defining features of AD, neuronal loss and synaptic pathology are closely related to the cognitive dysfunction. Brain imaging methods that are tuned to assess degeneration of myelinated nerve fibers in the brain (collectively called white matter) include diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and related techniques, and are expected to shed light on disease-related loss of structural connectivity. Participants ( $\mathrm{N}=70$, ages 47-76 years) from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Pre-vention study underwent DTI and hybrid diffusion imaging to determine a free-water elimina-tion (FWE-DTI) model. The study assessed the extent to which preclinical AD pathology affects brain white matter. Preclinical AD pathology was determined using cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers. The sample was enriched for AD risk (APOE $\varepsilon 4$ and parental history of AD). AD pathology assessed by CSF analyses was significantly associated with altered microstructure on both DTI and FWE-DTI. Affected regions included frontal, parietal, and especially temporal white matter. The $f$-value derived from the FWE-DTI model appeared to be the most sensitive to the relationship between the CSF AD biomarkers and microstruc-tural alterations in white matter. These findings suggest that white matter degeneration is an early pathological feature of AD that may have utility both for early disease detection and as outcome measures for clinical trials. Beyond standard volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), there are few options for gauging cell loss, and sensitive approaches [5]are needed, especially to measure early changes. Diffusion-weighted MRI is an increasingly used technique that is sensitive to the random self-diffusion of water molecules. In an unstructured medium, diffusion characteristics reflect properties of the fluid such as temperature and viscosity. However, in structured media such as brain tissue, the measured signals are instead modulated by the geometry of the tissue microstructure [6]. Thus, water molecules are used as a noninvasive endogenous tracer to probe tissue microstructure.

Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) describes the distribution of diffusion displacements using a Gaussian model and has been used extensively to assess tissue microstructure changes in aging, AD and preclinical AD [7-12]. Despite the promising sensitivity of DTI, it has known limitations that can impair utility and specific interpretation. To date, very few studies have applied advanced diffusion-weighted imaging methods for characterizing complex microstructural changes in the early stages of AD.

To date, very few studies have applied advanced diffusion-weighted imaging methods for characterizing complex microstructural changes in the early stages of AD. In this study, a free water elimination model was utilized to estimate and remove the signal contributions from cerebrospinal fluid and apparent free water components from the estimated diffusion tensor of the tissue. The FWE-DTI model contains an isotropic diffusion (free water) component with a diffusion coefficient that is constrained to be approximately three times larger than is typically encountered in tissue [13] in addition to the standard diffusion tensor. The free water diffusivity $\left(3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~mm}^{2} / \mathrm{s}\right)$ matches the theoretical diffusion coefficient of CSF at body temperature [14]. The free water signal fraction, denoted as the $f$-value, corresponds to the water that has minimal interaction with tissue barriers over the diffusion time of the experiment. This model minimizes the CSF contamination of DTI measurements in tissues adjacent to CSF filled spaces such as the ventricles and cerebral cortex [15], which is particularly important as brain atrophy increases with aging and disease burden. Non-zero $f$-values present in tissues distal from CSF may also reflect the relative volume of extracellular spaces in the tissue [13,16,17].

We hypothesize that FWE-DTI would provide improved sensitivity to microstructural alterations that occur early in the development of AD. In addition to shedding light on the early features of AD pathogenesis, focusing on microstructural alterations is important given that plaques and tangles-while central features of AD-may be accompanied by additional features that predict progression to dementia [4,18,19]. Greater sensitivity in detecting microstructural pathology may help identify individuals at greatest risk for cognitive decline, as well as providing a novel outcome measure for clinical trials.

Asymptomatic participants were recruited from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer's Prevention (WRAP) study[20], a cohort that is enriched for AD risk based on parental history of AD and a greater percentage of adults who carry a risk gene for AD, the $\varepsilon 4$ allele of apolipoprotein E

In addition to standard DTI participants underwent both hybrid diffusion imaging (HYDI) MRI [22] and lumbar puncture to assess levels of proteins related to AD and neurodegeneration in CSF. Biomarkers in CSF were used as a proxy for elevated preclinical AD pathology. CSF $\mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ was used as a marker of cortical amyloid deposition; $\mathrm{CSF} \mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ predicts conversion to AD dementia [23] and correlates with in vivo [24] amyloid burden measured with positron emission tomography. Phosphorylated tau (P-tau ${ }_{181}$ ) was used as a marker of neurofibrillary tangle load [25], and total tau (T-tau) as a marker of degeneration of thin unmyelinated axons. Both P-Tau and T-Tau are elevated in patients with dementia due to AD [26,27], P-tau ${ }_{181}$ discriminates AD from non-AD dementias [28] and higher levels of T-Tau are associated with a more rapid disease progression [29]. Neurofilament light chain protein (NFL) measured in CSF was used as a marker of large caliber axon degeneration [30], while YKL-40 and monocyte chemoattractant protein 1 (MCP-1) were used as markers of microglial activation and neuroinflammation [31]. Finally, we evaluated soluble amyloid precursor protein beta (sAPP $\beta$ ) as a marker of upstream APP processing in the $\beta$-secretase pathway [32]. We hypothesized that individuals with higher burden of preclinical AD pathology as shown by the CSF biomarkers would show microstructural alterations as measured by FWE-DTI.

Thus, microstructural white matter changes may be an early and measurable feature of the disease, and new methods for modeling complex diffusion are expected to be sensitive to this early pathology. We found significant associations between markers of AD pathology measured in CSF, and white matter microstructure, especially as indicated by FWE-DTI $f$-value. In particular, elevated ratios of $\mathrm{pTau} / \mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ and $\mathrm{tTau} / \mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ were robustly associated with higher free water or $f$-value in frontal and temporal lobe white matter. A novel marker of the amyloid pathway (sAPP $\beta$ ) also showed a robust association with altered microstructure as shown on FWE-DTI, especially when combined as a ratio with $\mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$. A similar correlation was seen with sAPP $\alpha$ as sAPP $\alpha$ and sAPP $\beta$ are themselves highly correlated.

The FWE model has been applied previously to a variety of cohorts including older individuals with mild cognitive impairment [71-73]. In these instances, the model was applied with the goal of removing confounding CSF effects, as it was here. Some have referred to the f-value as an indicator of atrophy [74,75]. However, the results here indicate that the f-value may be something more than simply the CSF fraction. Parenchymal f-values reported here (~40\%) are considerably higher than published reports from a similarly aged cohort (~7-9\%) [72]. It is important to consider that the previously mentioned studies use a single $\mathrm{b}=1000 \mathrm{~s} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ diffusion acquisition and heavily regularized fitting scheme [76]. It is likely that the difference in fvalue stems from the difference in acquisition schemes. Pasternak and colleagues have noted that using multishell acquisitions results in differences in estimated f-value [16]. While the difference presented here is much greater, so is the deviation in acquisition scheme. We also note that Bruggen et al. observed similar high free water values in their higher b-value multishell study of Alzheimer's disease[77]. It is well documented that diffusion in tissue at high b-values is decidedly non-Gaussian [78], which may be a significant factor in the elevated f-value.

Non-zero $f$-values that are measured in tissue distal from CSF may reflect the relative volume of extracellular space in the tissue. In the context of AD, this signal could be due to loss of axons, or loss of myelin in brain white matter. Roher et al have demonstrated substantial alteration in both myelin and axons in familial and sporadic AD [79,80]. The pathology of AD includes hyperphosphorylation of tau protein, resulting in axonal abnormalities and displacement of tau to neuronal cell bodies [81]. Markers in this study that were related to tau (tTau and pTau), in addition to NFL, were strongly associated with white matter microstructural features as shown on FWE-DTI. Given that tau and NFL are components of the axonal cytoskeleton, these results may suggest that the $f$-value is sensitive to early axonal degeneration. CSF markers and advanced multi-compartment imaging are expected to shed further light on the temporal sequence of axonal and myelin alteration in the course of AD [82].

It is also of interest that higher $\mathrm{sAPP} \beta / \mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ showed a widespread association with higher $f$ value across bilateral temporal and frontal white matter. Soluble $\mathrm{A} \beta-40$ and $\mathrm{A} \beta-42$ are elevated in white matter brain tissue assessed post mortem in AD patients compared to control [86]. APP cleavage by Beta-secretase 1 (BACE1) produces a membrane-bound fragment of APP that when further cleaved by $\gamma$-secretase yields several $\mathrm{A} \beta$ species including $\mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ ultimately leading to formation of deposited amyloid plaques [87]. Products of the $\beta$-secretase pathway include increases in amyloid- $\beta$ oligomers, which may be more toxic to neuronal cells than deposited plaques [88]. While CSF sAPP $\beta$ is not a direct measure of the oligomeric form of $\mathrm{A} \beta$, the $\mathrm{sAPP} \beta / \mathrm{A} \beta_{42}$ ratio may reflect both increased proteolytic processing of APP through the amyloidogenic pathway, as well as increased deposition of amyloid, providing a better marker of amyloid pathology than either measure alone. The ratio may also account for interindividual differences in APP production. To the author's knowledge, this is the first study showing a link between elevated $\beta$-secretase cleavage of APP and in vivo white matter abnormalities as shown on diffusion-weighted imaging in humans.

documents: The study found that standard and free-water diffusion tensor imaging (FW-DTI) both showed decreased fractional anisotropy (FA) in Alzheimer's disease, primarily in the corpus callosum and fornix, which is consistent with known neurodegenerative mechanisms.

While standard diffusion tensor imaging showed widespread higher axial and radial diffusivities, the FW-DTI model revealed that the free-water index was significantly elevated in these regions, indicating that free water contributions significantly impact standard metrics in neurodegenerative pathologies.

The authors interpret that FW-DTI provides improved consistency in FA, axial, and radial diffusivity metrics and better reflects the underlying pathology of Alzheimer's disease compared to standard diffusion tensor imaging.

Higher values of mode of anisotropy and fractional anisotropy were observed in the anterior thalamic radiation and cortico-spinal tract in Alzheimer's disease, which the authors attribute to a loss of crossing fibers.

Prior research using Free Water-Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FW-DTI) found that DTI-based markers of altered microstructure are significantly associated with cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers of preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology and that the FW index is associated with cognitive decline and elevated in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease patients compared to healthy controls.

The authors hypothesize that Free Water-Diffusion Tensor Imaging (FW-DTI) will improve the sensitivity and specificity for detecting white matter tract abnormalities in Alzheimer's disease by removing free water contributions, thereby providing a clearer and more specific interpretation of white matter pathology than standard DTI.

Prior diffusion tensor imaging studies found that Alzheimer's disease is associated with lower fractional anisotropy and higher axial and radial diffusivity values in white matter regions such as the corpus callosum, fornix, cingulum, and longitudinal fasciculi, suggesting these metrics may serve as early biomarkers preceding neuronal loss and symptom onset.

The relationship between diffusion tensor imaging metrics and cognitive scores is inconsistent across prior research, with some studies showing significant correlations while others do not, which the authors interpret as evidence of methodologic or analytic impacts on the data.

The authors note that standard diffusion tensor imaging suffers from partial volume effects, where metrics reflect a weighted average of multiple tissue types rather than specific white matter integrity, a limitation that is particularly profound in Alzheimer's disease due to secondary increases in cerebrospinal fluid and free water resulting from neuronal loss.

To address the confounding effects of extracellular free water on diffusion metrics, the authors highlight the development of a free water correction algorithm that improves tissue specificity and tract reconstruction, a model previously applied to study Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and depression.

The application of Free Water (FW)-DTI for Alzheimer's Disease (AD) better reflects the underlying pathology of white matter neurodegenerative processes and should further improve the interpretation of AD white matter pathology.
The study found significant clusters where free-water index values were higher in Alzheimer's disease patients compared to healthy controls, with no clusters showing the opposite pattern.

The analysis identified specific brain locations where significant differences between groups were found for both standard and free-water DTI analyses, including the fornix, corpus callosum, and cingulum.

In Alzheimer's disease patients compared to healthy controls, lower fractional anisotropy was observed primarily in the fornix and corpus callosum, while higher fractional anisotropy was found in the right anterior thalamic radiation, cortical spinal tract, posterior limb of internal capsule, and superior corona radiata.

Alzheimer's disease patients exhibited significantly higher axial and radial diffusivity values than healthy controls across all significant clusters, with no regions showing lower diffusivity values in the disease group.

The fornix, corpus callosum, forceps minor, and left cingulum showed a specific pattern of white matter alteration where lower fractional anisotropy overlapped with higher axial and radial diffusivity.

Standard DTI analysis found that only clusters with higher axial and radial diffusivities in Alzheimer's disease compared to healthy controls were significant, with substantial overlap in the cingulum, fornix, and sagittal stratum.
FW-DTI analysis revealed that lower fractional anisotropy in Alzheimer's disease was localized to the fornix and corpus callosum, but these clusters were smaller than those identified by standard FA.

Unlike standard DTI, FW-DTI showed both higher and lower values for axial and radial diffusivities in the Alzheimer's disease group, with lower axial diffusivity observed in the corpus callosum and fornix and higher axial diffusivity in the anterior thalamic radiation, corticospinal tract, and retrolenticular part of the internal capsule.

FW-DTI results indicated that lower fractional anisotropy in the Alzheimer's disease group overlapped with lower axial and radial diffusivities in the fornix, and with lower axial diffusivity in the corpus callosum and forceps minor.

Higher fractional anisotropy in the Alzheimer's disease group overlapped with higher axial diffusivity and lower radial diffusivity in the superior fronto-occipital fasciculus, right posterior limb of the internal capsule, superior cerebellar peduncle, and anterior limb of the internal capsule.

FW-DTI analysis did not identify any clusters where both axial and radial diffusivities were simultaneously higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, a finding that contrasts with the standard DTI results.

Higher fractional anisotropy (FW) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) compared to healthy controls (HC) was observed widespread across cerebral white matter, with no significant clusters found where HC had higher FW than AD.

Significant differences in the FW index between AD and HC were observed in several white matter regions, most prominently the fornix, cingulum (both hippocampal and cingulate gyrus parts), and the corpus callosum.

Significantly higher mean anisotropy (MA) values in AD compared to healthy controls were observed in the right corticospinal tract, right posterior limb of the internal capsule, right sagittal stratum, and right superior fronto-occipital fasciculus, indicating more linear anisotropy.
Lower mean anisotropy (MA) values in AD compared to healthy controls were found mainly in the genu of the corpus callosum and in the external capsule, corresponding to more planar anisotropy.

The study found that fractional anisotropy (FW) values were significantly higher in Alzheimer's disease (AD) subjects compared to healthy controls (HC) across multiple white matter tracts, including the cingulum (hippocampal part), fornix, and corpus callosum. These findings indicate that AD is associated with increased anisotropy in specific brain regions, a result that was consistent across both standard DTI and FW-DTI analyses.

The authors observed that the mean anisotropy (MA) index showed significant differences between healthy controls and Alzheimer's disease subjects, with specific clusters indicating where MA was higher in AD compared to HC. This pattern of increased MA in AD subjects was confirmed using both standard DTI and FW-DTI methods, suggesting a robust association between the disease and altered tissue anisotropy.

No significant voxel-based correlation was found between the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score and either standard or fiber-orientation-aware (FW) diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics. The correlations between fractional anisotropy (FA) and other DTI metrics, such as axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), increased substantially after FW correction, indicating that older healthy control participants have substantial fiber-orientation contributions to their dMRI-derived metrics.

Free water-corrected axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity metrics were found to be more consistent with pathology-based expected spatial patterns of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease patients than standard metrics. The authors interpret this finding as evidence that the free water correction method improves the accuracy and sensitivity of diffusion tensor imaging metrics in Alzheimer's disease.

The study found that raw diffusivity parameters, specifically axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity, are more impacted by intravoxel free-water diffusion than the composite metric of fractional anisotropy. This biophysical difference explains why axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity show striking differences between standard and free water-corrected measurements compared to fractional anisotropy.

Significant white matter differences were observed between healthy controls and Alzheimer's disease subjects in several regions using both standard and free water-corrected diffusion tensor imaging metrics. The free water index was higher in Alzheimer's disease participants than in healthy controls across many regions, which aligns with expected neurodegenerative changes.

The application of Free Water (FW) correction in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) improves the accuracy and sensitivity of Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) metrics, confirming that lower Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and higher Mean Diffusivity (MD) in the fornix reflect true pathological changes rather than artifacts from partial volume effects or atrophy.

FW-corrected DTI reveals large clusters of lower Fractional Anisotropy (FA) in the genu and body of the corpus callosum (CC) with minimal splenial changes, a pattern that supports the anterior-to-posterior progression of the retrogenesis hypothesis over the posterior-to-anterior progression of Wallerian degeneration.

Paradoxical increases in Fractional Anisotropy (FA) and Mean Anisotropy (MA) in the anterior thalamic radiation (ATR), corticospinal tract (CST), and internal capsule in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) indicate the loss of crossing fiber populations, which standard DTI methods fail to resolve due to the assumption of Gaussian diffusion.

FW-DTI revealed lower axial diffusivity in white matter regions corresponding to lower fractional anisotropy, suggesting that prior reports of higher axial diffusivity in Alzheimer's disease were likely artifacts caused by free water contamination rather than true tissue changes.

The authors interpret the higher free water volume fraction in Alzheimer's disease patients as indicative of sub-voxel neurodegenerative processes and potential loss of white matter integrity, particularly in the fornix and corpus callosum.

The study found no significant voxel-wise correlations between MMSE scores and DTI metrics, which the authors attribute to the narrow range of cognitive scores in the predominantly mild Alzheimer's cohort, but they suggest that FW-corrected metrics offer a methodological improvement for future studies linking white matter integrity to cognitive function.

The authors conclude that diffusion kurtosis imaging metrics provide more sensitive and specific insight into Alzheimer's disease-related pathological changes in white matter compared to other metrics.

The study found that FW-DTI identified white matter changes in Alzheimer's disease that were more consistent with known pathology in both magnitude and direction than standard DTI approaches. The authors interpret this to mean that FW correction improves the sensitivity and specificity of DTI metrics by removing partial volume effects, thereby providing more reliable insight into AD-related pathological changes.

The authors note that no significant correlations were observed between DTI metrics and the MMSE score, a finding consistent with previous studies. They interpret this lack of correlation to suggest that the relationship between global cognitive scores and white matter pathology in Alzheimer's disease may not be linear.

The authors propose that the Fiber Orientation (FW) index may improve sensitivity to sub-voxel neurodegeneration, while the Mean Anisotropy (MA) metric may improve specificity related to crossing fibers. These specific contributions are interpreted as enhancing the overall reliability and inter-parameter consistency of DTI metrics in the presence of atrophy.

The study's core finding of a potential therapeutic effect is downgraded to hypothesis-generating status because the unspecified spending function undermines the validity of the final p-value, meaning the precise magnitude of the benefit cannot be trusted.

The claim of significant improvement is unsupported by the current evidence because the potential observer bias from unblinded raters prevents distinguishing true efficacy from measurement error, a limitation that is more consequential than the statistical spending function issue.

The methodological opacity regarding whether raters were blinded to treatment allocation creates a critical gap that prevents the raw outcome data from being comparable to prior work, as observer expectation may have inflated the treatment effect independently of the statistical analysis.

xD was found to be sensitive to microstructural alterations in white matter associated with cognitive decline during the transition from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease, suggesting it may serve as a valuable biomarker for early detection and monitoring of Alzheimer's disease progression.
Longitudinal diffusion tensor imaging analyses provide critical insights into the temporal dynamics of white matter degeneration and its role in clinical deterioration in Alzheimer's disease.

While structural MRI is used to visualize brain atrophy in Alzheimer's disease, it exhibits limitations in detecting subtle white matter damage in early stages, whereas diffusion tensor imaging can detect microstructural changes and the integrity of white matter tracts.

Axial diffusivity can detect axonal degeneration, whereas radial diffusivity can detect changes related to demyelination, allowing these diffusivity metrics to comprehensively evaluate distinct pathological mechanisms in white matter.

The study found significant increases in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity over two years in widespread white matter tracts, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, corona radiata, cingulum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and fornix, in patients transitioning from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease.

Changes in axial diffusivity, particularly in the left retrolenticular internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus, showed significant correlations with cognitive decline, whereas radial diffusivity changes were not significantly associated with clinical dementia rating score changes in any region.

Multivariate regression analysis identified axial diffusivity in the left retrolenticular internal capsule as a significant independent predictor of cognitive decline, suggesting that axial diffusivity is a sensitive biomarker for microstructural white matter alterations associated with the transition from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease.

The authors excluded fractional anisotropy (FA) from correlation and regression analyses because FA is a composite metric that lacks the specificity needed to isolate distinct pathological mechanisms, whereas axial and radial diffusivity (AxD and RD) better elucidate microstructural changes in Alzheimer's disease.

Region-of-interest (ROI) analyses targeting the cingulum, corpus callosum, and uncinate fasciculus were conducted in an exploratory, post hoc manner based on significant whole-brain findings, requiring cautious interpretation as they were not derived from a priori hypotheses.

The study hypothesized that increased Axonal Damage (AxD) and Radial Diffusivity (RD) values represent early pathological changes, such as axonal degeneration and demyelination, during the progression from Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Additionally, the authors hypothesized that longitudinal changes in AxD and RD are associated with cognitive decline.

The authors interpret that longitudinal analyses of AxD and RD can elucidate the progression of White Matter (WM) damage and its causal relationship with cognitive decline, potentially establishing WM damage as an early marker for Alzheimer's Disease (AD). This approach addresses the limitations of previous cross-sectional studies by capturing the dynamic nature of WM changes over time.
The study found a statistically significant increase in the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score over two years, indicating substantial cognitive decline in the participants.

The study found that axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD) values in the corpus callosum exhibited extensive changes, with the largest increases in AxD observed in the superior longitudinal fasciculus and posterior corona radiata.

Widespread increases in white matter diffusivity metrics in regions such as the internal capsule, corona radiata, and cingulum cingulate gyrus indicate considerable microstructural changes during the two-year follow-up period.

TBSS analysis revealed a significant increase in axial diffusivity and radial diffusivity values across extensive brain regions, including the corpus callosum, internal capsule, and fornix, when compared to baseline observations.
The study participants' Clinical Dementia Rating scores significantly increased from a baseline mean of 2.42 to a follow-up mean of 4.64, indicating disease progression over the study period.

Axial diffusivity (AxD) changes exhibited the strongest correlation with changes in the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) score, with significant associations found in the left retrolenticular part of the internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix cres stria terminalis, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus.

Changes in axial diffusivity (AxD) in the left retrolenticular internal capsule were significantly associated with changes in the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR), while AxD changes in the right superior longitudinal fasciculus, right sagittal stratum, left superior longitudinal fasciculus, and left posterior thalamic radiation showed weak positive trends that were not statistically significant.
No significant correlations were observed between changes in radial diffusivity (RD) and changes in CDR scores across any of the examined white matter regions.

TBSS analysis revealed a significant increase in AxD and RD in several white matter regions, including the corpus callosum, cingulum, and superior longitudinal fasciculus, with the widespread increase in AxD correlating with cognitive decline while RD changes did not significantly associate with cognitive decline.

The authors interpret these findings to indicate that an increase in AxD is closely related to cognitive decline, suggesting that damage to specific white matter tracts like the corpus callosum and cingulum leads to cognitive and functional impairments by disrupting interhemispheric communication and limbic system connections.

The study's findings align with prior cross-sectional and longitudinal work that reported increases in AxD and RD in the corpus callosum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and cingulum in Alzheimer's disease patients, as well as previous reports of correlations between cognitive scores and diffusivity changes in the posterior cingulum.

Axonal degeneration in the left retrolenticular region of the internal capsule, left posterior corona radiata, left fornix, and right superior longitudinal fasciculus significantly correlates with cognitive decline, a finding consistent with prior research linking these temporal lobe and limbic pathways to memory and executive function.

The absence of significant correlations between radial diffusivity changes and cognitive decline suggests that axonal degeneration, rather than myelin integrity loss, is the predominant driver of clinical progression at this stage of Alzheimer's disease.

The authors interpret the observed increases in axial diffusivity as reflecting Wallerian degeneration and severe tissue loss, noting that axonal damage emerges earlier than demyelination in the disease timeline.

Multivariate regression analysis confirmed that axial diffusivity changes in the left retrolenticular internal capsule independently correlate with cognitive decline, while other regions showed only minor positive trends.

AxD changes, particularly in the left retrolenticular IC, serve as independent predictors of cognitive decline, reinforcing the hypothesis that axonal damage is the primary driver of microstructural alterations in AD progression. In contrast, RD changes across all examined WM regions were not substantially associated with cognitive decline, suggesting that myelin loss may not be the primary driver of disease progression.

The authors interpret AxD as a reliable marker for identifying and monitoring the initial progression of AD because it reflects early pathological progression, whereas RD changes become more prominent in later stages of the disease. This longitudinal analysis provides a clearer understanding of the temporal progression of microstructural changes and their association with cognitive decline compared to previous cross-sectional studies.

The authors note that AxD values have been inconsistently reported across studies due to multiple pathological processes affecting the metric, and they acknowledge that the reliance on simplified diffusion tensor model assumptions may not fully capture the complexity of actual WM structures.

A significant correlation was observed between white matter microstructural changes, specifically assessed using diffusion metrics like axial diffusivity (AxD) and radial diffusivity (RD), and cognitive decline during the progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease.
The study found that an increase in AxD is particularly prevalent and strongly associated with changes in cognitive status, suggesting AxD may be a sensitive indicator of early pathological changes.

The authors interpret the findings to highlight the utility of AxD as a potential biomarker for the early detection and monitoring of Alzheimer's disease progression, providing insights into the distinct roles of white matter diffusion metrics in reflecting axonal and myelin pathology.

The study's primary endpoint is fundamentally uninterpretable because the methods section fails to specify rater blinding status or the clinical scale acquisition protocol, making it impossible to isolate whether the reported effect stems from treatment efficacy or observer bias.

The study extends prior work by suggesting a potential therapeutic signal, but the authors' claim of efficacy remains an assumption rather than a confirmed finding because the subjective endpoints and invalid multiplicity adjustments prevent verification of the actual effect size.
Neuronal loss and synaptic pathology are more strongly related to dementia severity and cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's disease than beta-amyloid plaques or neurofibrillary tangles.

Diffusion-weighted MRI is used as a sensitive technique to measure early brain changes and cell loss in Alzheimer's disease by probing tissue microstructure through the random self-diffusion of water molecules.
Complex models of microstructural diffusion, such as FWE-DTI, may provide increased sensitivity to early brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease compared to standard DTI.
AD pathology assessed by cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers was significantly associated with altered microstructure in frontal, parietal, and especially temporal white matter regions.

The f-value derived from the free-water elimination (FWE-DTI) model appeared to be the most sensitive metric for detecting the relationship between cerebrospinal fluid AD biomarkers and white matter microstructural alterations.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence that white matter degeneration is an early pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting potential utility for early disease detection and as outcome measures for clinical trials.
The FWE-DTI signal model uses two non-zero b-values to simplify the parameter space, which allows for accurate and stable diffusion measures even without spatial constraints or assumptions.
Using FWE-DTI tensors instead of standard DTI tensors ensured a more complete reconstruction of the fornix.
The FWE-DTI implementation uses two non-zero b-values to simplify the parameter space, allowing for accurate and stable diffusion measures without requiring spatial constraints or assumptions.

The study hypothesized that individuals with a higher burden of preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology, indicated by cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, would exhibit microstructural alterations measured by FWE-DTI.

Cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers were utilized as proxies for preclinical Alzheimer's disease pathology, with CSF Aβ42 serving as a marker for cortical amyloid deposition and phospho-tau 181 serving as a marker for neurofibrillary tangle load.

Total tau and neurofilament light chain protein were used as markers for degeneration of thin unmyelinated axons and large caliber axon degeneration respectively, while YKL-40 and MCP-1 served as markers for microglial activation and neuroinflammation.

The authors hypothesize that the free water elimination diffusion tensor imaging (FWE-DTI) model provides improved sensitivity to microstructural alterations occurring early in the development of Alzheimer's disease compared to standard diffusion tensor imaging.

Standard diffusion tensor imaging has known limitations that can impair its utility and specific interpretation, and very few studies have previously applied advanced diffusion-weighted imaging methods to characterize complex microstructural changes in the early stages of Alzheimer's disease.

The FWE-DTI model is designed to minimize cerebrospinal fluid contamination of diffusion tensor measurements in tissues adjacent to CSF-filled spaces, which is particularly important as brain atrophy increases with aging and disease burden.
Non-zero free water signal fractions (f-values) found in tissues distant from cerebrospinal fluid may reflect the relative volume of extracellular spaces within the tissue.

Detecting microstructural pathology with greater sensitivity may help identify individuals at the greatest risk for cognitive decline and provide a novel outcome measure for clinical trials, complementing the assessment of plaques and tangles.

The APOE4+ group displayed a lower mean Aβ42 value compared to the APOE4- group, while none of the CSF markers were significantly associated with sex or parental family history of Alzheimer's disease.
The study utilized a false discovery rate threshold of p ≤ 0.05 to control for multiple comparisons when analyzing the effect of biomarkers on seven tracts and diffusion metrics.
A voxel-based analysis was performed across white matter and the hippocampus, with the hippocampal mask derived from the Desikan probabilistic structural atlas warped to the population atlas space.

The voxel-based analysis controlled for age and sex while testing the main effect of each biomarker on diffusion metrics, using a family wise error threshold of p ≤ 0.05 to account for multiple comparisons.

The study found that associations between CSF biomarkers and white matter were largely located in temporal and frontal regions, with only DTI MD and FWE-DTI f-value metrics showing significant positive relations to the biomarkers.

For both imaging methods, the largest significant cluster included the left temporal lobe, though the FWE-DTI cluster spread more diffusely, and significant association regions showed substantial overlap among different biomarker comparisons.
No significant effects were observed for either diffusion method within the hippocampus.

The study found that diffusion metrics along the posterior portions of the corpus callosum (CC-III, CC-IV, and CC-V) were the only regions of interest showing an association with CSF biomarkers, including pTau181, tTau, and YKL-40, as well as their ratios to Aβ42. The authors note that these associations were most robust for the ratios of markers rather than individual markers, although no correlations remained significant after false discovery rate correction.

In the FWE-DTI analysis, the f-value metric showed a positive correlation with CSF biomarkers, specifically affecting the cingulum bundles and CC-I, with relationships observed for pTau181 and the ratios of pTau181, tTau, YKL-40, and sAPPβ to Aβ42. The voxel-based analysis revealed widespread areas where diffusion metrics were related to the ratios of pTau181, tTau, and sAPPβ to Aβ42 in both DTI and FWE-DTI analyses, while pTau181 was significantly correlated with diffusion measures only in the FWE-DTI analysis.

The study found that significant regions of association in the DTI MD analysis showed substantial overlap with previous findings, while no significant effects were observed for either diffusion method within the hippocampus.

The FWE-DTI tractography analysis identified significant associations between cerebrospinal fluid biomarker ratios, such as pTau181/Aβ42 and sAPP/Aβ42, and fractional anisotropy in specific white matter tracts including the corpus callosum and cingulum.

Significant clusters correlating with the pTau181/Aβ42 biomarker ratio were found in the left and right fusiform gyrus white matter, as well as the left and right inferior temporal gyrus white matter, indicating widespread white matter involvement associated with this specific biomarker profile.
The study found that altered white matter microstructure was not a significant predictor of cognitive test performance in the context of preclinical Alzheimer's disease.
Among six cognitive test scores assessed, only the Trails B test showed a modest relationship with mean f-value, but this relationship did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

The authors interpret these findings as part of a broader effort to understand pathological features in the earliest stages of Alzheimer's disease, which may serve as targets for treatment or for identifying candidates for clinical trials before significant cell loss occurs.

The study found that elevated ratios of pTau181/Aβ42 and tTau181/Aβ42 in cerebrospinal fluid were robustly associated with higher free water or f-value in frontal and temporal lobe white matter, indicating that microstructural white matter changes are an early and measurable feature of Alzheimer's disease.

A novel marker of the amyloid pathway, sAPPβ, showed a robust association with altered white matter microstructure, particularly when combined as a ratio with Aβ42, and a similar correlation was observed with sAPPα due to the high correlation between these two proteins.

The current study extends prior work by demonstrating that the FWE-DTI method demonstrates greater sensitivity to associations between Alzheimer's pathology and white matter microstructure compared to standard DTI, which previously showed associations between tau and Aβ42 ratios and mean diffusivity.

Analysis of hippocampal gray matter showed no association with Alzheimer's pathology markers, suggesting that preclinical Alzheimer's pathology may be detectable in white matter prior to changes in hippocampal microstructure or volume.

The study found hippocampal alteration that persists even when using diffusion-weighted measures, which are potentially more sensitive to subtle changes than T1-weighted imaging. The authors interpret the high parenchymal f-values (approximately 40%) as indicating something more than just CSF fraction, noting that these values are considerably higher than published reports from similarly aged cohorts (approximately 7-9%) and likely stem from differences in acquisition schemes and non-Gaussian diffusion at high b-values.
Higher levels of pTau181/Aβ42 were associated with higher DTI mean diffusivity primarily in the left and right temporal lobes.

CSF markers related to tau (tTau and pTau) and neurofilament light chain (NFL) were strongly associated with white matter microstructural features, suggesting that the f-value is sensitive to early axonal degeneration in Alzheimer's disease.

The study found robust associations between CSF biomarkers reflecting core Alzheimer's pathology and white matter microstructure, linking amyloid pathology to axonal degeneration through mechanisms such as Aβ42 toxicity and leakage into neurons.

Tractography analysis revealed a suggestive positive association between mean diffusivity and YKL-40, a marker of microglial activation, indicating that inflammation may increase neuronal cell vulnerability, although these results did not survive multiple comparison correction.

The study found that Alzheimer's disease pathology was robustly associated with altered diffusion in bilateral temporal and frontal lobes, regions known to be involved in the early stages of the disease.
These findings contribute to a growing body of literature indicating that white matter degeneration is likely an early and measurable feature of Alzheimer's disease.

The study found that the sAPPβ/Aβ42 ratio showed a widespread association with higher f values across bilateral temporal and frontal white matter, which the authors interpret as reflecting increased proteolytic processing of APP through the amyloidogenic pathway and increased amyloid deposition.

The authors state that their work is the first study to demonstrate a link between elevated β-secretase cleavage of APP and in vivo white matter abnormalities visualized via diffusion-weighted imaging in humans.

The study concludes that markers of Alzheimer's disease pathology are associated with microstructural white matter alteration, an improvement upon prior DTI studies achieved by employing a FWE-DTI approach to model complex water diffusion in cerebral white matter.

The primary outcome measure's acquisition parameters are entirely unspecified, with the authors failing to report the psychometric properties of the scale or the specific training protocols for the raters. This opacity in the measurement process means the data collection is unverified before statistical analysis, undermining the validity of any observed effects.

The study is characterized as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory, yet it remains a black box for independent verification because the authors did not release the raw scores and rater logs. Without these specific artifacts, it is impossible to distinguish a true effect from observer bias or to reproduce the analysis to test alternative hypotheses.

The central finding of the Alzheimer's brain scan study is effectively uninterpretable because the underlying measurement error variance is undefined, meaning the reported signal cannot be distinguished from noise or observer bias.

The study's validity is compromised by a distinct methodological flaw where post hoc ROI selection creates a circular reasoning risk, biasing the spatial localization of the signal independently of the missing psychometric properties.

The main finding of early white matter changes via free-water DTI cannot be integrated with prior volumetric literature because the missing acquisition details and statistical corrections prevent determining whether the result genuinely extends previous findings or conflicts with them due to methodological artifacts.

While the free-water correction offers a more precise tool for detecting microstructural changes, the authors interpret its current utility as limited by unresolved methodological artifacts and a lack of replication data. Consequently, the study provides a promising hint for earlier detection rather than a definitive conclusion on standalone clinical utility until the preprocessing pipeline is verified.

The study suggests a new scan method might spot early memory-related changes sooner than standard tests, but it does not prove this method is superior to current diagnostic tools. The authors interpret the results as a promising hint rather than a confirmed improvement, emphasizing that there is insufficient proof that using this new scan leads to better clinical outcomes or that patients should alter their current care plans.

The available evidence is fragmented, with different studies failing to align on whether the new scan method accurately identifies disease progression or merely introduces confusing noise. The consensus interpretation is that the current data is inconclusive, and the only way to determine the true accuracy of the method is through a large-scale study using standardized tools and open data to directly compare the results against clinical outcomes.
